### Seminole Tribe — March 27, 1996

**Judgment and remedy.**

| Component | Disposition and vote | Supporting Justices | Opposing Justices | Operative effect |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Governor Chiles | Reversed and remanded, 5–4 | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer | O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas | Remove the categorical bar to the connected officer action; retain IGRA's conditions and lawful prospective limits. |
| Florida | Immunity-dismissal direction set aside and remanded, 5–4 as to this common relief | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer | O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas | Remove that appellate command without a majority holding establishing State amenability. |

The Florida component contains three distinct primary positions: Stone-Zsela and Stevens would reverse and sustain the direct State action; Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer would vacate without deciding amenability; O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas would affirm. The first five share removal of the dismissal direction and remand, not a constitutional or avoidance rationale. Stone-Zsela expressly disagrees with stopping short of sustaining the State action.

The State claim is not terminated by the immunity ruling. This mandate supplies no majority determination establishing jurisdiction over Florida and no finding that jurisdiction is absent. Any State merits adjudication requires a lawful jurisdictional basis. The three Justices' additional avoidance sequencing is not a Court instruction. The separate September 1993 merits judgment and stayed appeal are not vacated, decided or treated as an undecided district-court merits action. No bad faith, compact, gaming entitlement, license, damages or taxing power is awarded.

**Opinion topology.**

| Writing or component | Author | Joined by | Scope and relationship to judgment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court, Part I | Souter | O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer | Seven Justices reject the categorical Article III objection. Stevens retains serious doubt; Stone-Zsela does not join this explanation. |
| Opinion of the Court, Parts II–III | Souter | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Ginsburg and Breyer | Five Justices adopt the IGRA-specific officer route and its statutory and remedial limits. |
| Florida judgment announcement and shared remand | Souter | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Ginsburg and Breyer as to the common operative relief | Five support setting aside the immunity-dismissal direction. Stone-Zsela and Stevens agree with that component of the judgment only; they additionally would sustain direct-State amenability. |
| Opinion respecting the State claim, Part IV | Souter | Ginsburg and Breyer throughout | Three prefer avoidance and explain an alternative common-law/Article I analysis. The alternative's activation condition is absent; it supplies no actual abrogation joins. |
| Opinion concurring in part and dissenting in part | Stone-Zsela | No other Justice | Joins Parts II–III and common State removal; would additionally sustain the prospective direct-State action and rejects treating officer availability as sufficient reason to withhold that relief. |
| Opinion concurring in part and dissenting in part | Stevens | No other Justice | Joins Parts II–III and common State removal; would sustain the State action on his broader nontextual-immunity ground; retains serious Article III doubt without an independent dismissal vote. |
| Opinion concurring in part and dissenting in part | O'Connor | Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas throughout | All four join Part I; they would affirm both immunity dismissals, overrule Union Gas's constitutional conclusion and exclude the officer route under this statute. |

Six Justices—Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas—actually adopt unmistakable direct-State statutory intent in their separate writings. The other three accept that proposition only in their unused alternative. This agreement concerns statutory authorization, not constitutional power. No aggregation of conditional votes or broader separate reasons supplies a controlling State-amenability rule.

**Holdings and complete conditions.**

### I. The statutory judicial decision is not categorically advisory

**Controlling proposition:** Adjudicating IGRA's federal good-faith negotiation dispute is a judicial function where the judgment conclusively determines the parties' legal relations and activates constrained statutory consequences. The prospect of later mediation and executive action, and the absence of a guaranteed compact, do not make the court's decision merely advisory.

**Authority:** Part I has seven direct supporters: O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. Stevens's serious reservation is not an eighth join; Stone-Zsela supplies no independent join.

**Controlling explanation:** A court decides an existing dispute over a federal duty and, upon the requisite finding, changes the parties' legal obligations and access to the next statutory stage. That supplies effective partial relief even though neither the desired compact nor every desired game is assured. The decision's legal operation matters; the answer does not rest solely on whether the Secretary can edit individual findings.

Aetna and Nashville reject a universal requirement that judicial relief take the form of an immediately executable coercive decree. Brimson supports judicial adjudication in aid of administration, while its actual enforceable-order setting prevents treating it as an answer to every intermediate proceeding. Ferreira and the relevant Gordon and Hayburn materials require attention to whether the purported judgment has legal effect or remains subject to executive revision. IGRA's binding determination and prescribed consequences satisfy that concern here.

Wisconsin's partial-redress reasoning offers a limited analogy, not a prior adjudication of this judicial-function question. Morgan Stanley/Plaut's protection of completed judgments likewise supplies no universal answer. The Court neither determines every later preclusion question nor manufactures coercive remedies or a new cause of action to make the statutory decision judicial.

### II. IGRA permits this connected officer action within its own limits

**Controlling proposition:** Ex parte Young permits a prospective official-capacity action against Governor Chiles to enforce an ongoing violation of IGRA's good-faith negotiating duty, subject to the statute's full sequence and remedial limitations. IGRA's State-directed wording and detailed procedure do not exclude that route in this case.

**Authority:** Part II has five direct supporters: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer. The common rule is specific to IGRA; it does not adopt the three Justices' additional general clear-indication theory.

**Controlling explanation:** Young provides the established route against a responsible officer for an ongoing federal violation. The Governor's representatives participated in negotiations, supplying the required connection to the alleged failure. Rejecting categorical dismissal does not require proof that he alone can bind Florida to every compact term. Mandatory good faith differs from discretion over those terms.

Congress imposed a federal negotiating duty and prescribed how its enforcement progresses. References to the State do not, in this arrangement, exclude the official through whom its obligations are performed. The scheme limits the officer action rather than authorizing a free-standing injunction with greater remedies. This construction answers the objection that an officer could evade Congress's chosen restraints: both sixty-day periods, mediation, selection, consent and Secretarial conditions remain effective. It does not treat remedial detail as irrelevant or establish that every statutory right carries officer relief.

The State's involvement in negotiations establishes neither waiver nor unlimited compacting authority. Incorporation of state gaming law into the federal obligation does not itself convert the claim into a Pennhurst demand to enforce state law. Hafer's individual-capacity damages rule supplies no basis for this action, and Edelman's retrospective-relief boundary remains.

The actual request for a compact and declaration does not establish entitlement to either. A court cannot prescribe its preferred compact, enlarge the good-faith duty, bypass mediation or recast accrued compensation as an injunction. The statutory progression, rather than an added coercive order compelling agreement, governs failure to reach agreement. The categorical officer dismissal must therefore be reversed while the remaining merits and lawful relief receive their proper treatment.

### III. Removing the officer bar does not establish the predicates for compacting relief

**Controlling proposition:** The remand permits only relief authorized by IGRA upon the actual statutory predicates. It neither resolves good faith or gaming scope nor disturbs the distinct merits judgment and appeal. The following conditions govern any relief through the recognized officer route.

**Authority:** Part III has the same five direct supporters. The four opposing the route preserve the same enacted conditions in their dissent; recognizing those conditions does not imply their agreement to reversal.

**Controlling explanation:** A valid duty, an available enforcement defendant and entitlement to a particular remedy are different questions. IGRA makes adverse findings, successive waiting periods and specified mediation and administrative steps do separate work. Removing immunity cannot substitute for any of them. Nor does the actual prayer enlarge the relief Congress supplied. The September 1993 merits judgment and its stayed appeal must receive their own lawful disposition; this immunity mandate decides neither. The Court accordingly preserves the statutory progression and independent gaming conditions below without ordering that progression to begin as though bad faith were already established.

**Complete statutory conditions and limits:**

- Under 25 U.S.C. §2710(d)(3)(A), a qualifying request by the Tribe with jurisdiction over the relevant Indian lands triggers the State's duty to negotiate in good faith, not a duty to accept preferred terms. A failure-to-negotiate suit under (d)(7)(A)(i) may begin only after 180 days. The effective-compact enforcement action under (A)(ii) and Secretary's enforcement action under (A)(iii) remain distinct.
- Under (B)(ii), tribal evidence that no compact exists and that the State failed to respond or respond in good faith precedes the State's burden to prove good faith. Nonagreement alone does not establish bad faith. An actual adverse finding triggers (B)(iii)'s order to the State and Tribe to conclude a compact within the first sixty-day period. The court **may** consider public interest, public safety, criminality, financial integrity and adverse economic effects on existing gaming; it **shall** consider a demand for direct taxation of the Tribe or Indian lands as evidence of bad faith.
- If no agreement follows during that period, (B)(iv) requires each side's last-best proposal to a court-appointed mediator. The mediator selects the proposal best comporting with IGRA, other applicable federal law, and the court's findings and order. Submission to both parties under (B)(v) begins a **second sixty-day period** for State consent. Consent makes the proposal an agreed compact under (B)(vi).
- Nonconsent during that second period triggers notice to the Secretary under (B)(vii). The Secretary **shall** prescribe procedures, consulting the Tribe and acting consistently with the selected proposal, IGRA and relevant state law. The express findings/order selection criterion appears in (iv), not verbatim in (vii). The Secretary lacks unrestricted discretion to withhold all action after the enacted predicates occur.
- State nonparticipation does not automatically select the Tribe's proposal. The government's qualified prediction supplies no textual default. The adopted construction adds neither contempt nor an order compelling agreement merely because agreement or participation during the ordered period fails; statutory progression is the consequence. No rule concerning every separate obstruction or disobedience sanction is decided.
- Section (d)(4) grants no new state taxing power while preserving regulatory-cost assessments agreed under (d)(3)(C)(iii). That exception is distinct from the mandatory treatment of direct-tax demands as bad-faith evidence. Absence of other taxing authority does not justify refusing negotiation.
- Class III gaming still requires approved tribal legislation, a State permitting such gaming for some person, organization or entity, and an effective compact subject to applicable remedial provisions; licensing and regulation remain separate. Under (d)(8), disapproval may rest on IGRA violations, other federal law **not relating to jurisdiction over gaming on Indian lands**, or federal trust obligations. Forty-five-day inaction produces approval only insofar as consistent with IGRA; Federal Register publication remains necessary.
- Section 2721's severability provision preserves qualifying remaining law but does not satisfy a finding, waiting period, mediation, selection or nonconsent condition and creates no alternative program. The distinct asserted Secretary substitute remedy remains unadjudicated. The Court neither endorses an automatic bypass nor reverses the lower court's separate substitute-remedy determination. Immunity dismissal alone satisfies none of the enacted predicates.

### IV. Direct-State intent is agreed upon, but State amenability is unresolved

**Majority-supported statutory proposition:** IGRA unmistakably authorizes a direct action naming the State. Its specified State-party action, State evidentiary burden, order to State and Tribe and successive State-directed steps satisfy the clear-statement requirement. General federal-question jurisdiction, §1362 or scattered references to States alone would not suffice.

**Authority and force:** Stone-Zsela, Stevens and the four dissenters actually adopt this statutory construction across their writings. Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer accept it only if their alternative State route must be reached. The six-position agreement establishes only the exact statutory-authorization proposition stated above; it creates no common State-amenability opinion. Statutory intent and constitutional authority remain separate: no controlling holding sustains or rejects Florida's amenability, and no majority opinion decides the constitutional question. It also supplies no sequencing rule requiring abrogation to be decided before officer relief.

**Common judgment, without common State rationale:** Five support setting aside the immunity-dismissal direction and remand. Two support affirmative direct-State relief; three support nonmerits vacatur; four oppose either change. Avoidance is not a logical subset of the two Justices' affirmative constitutional grounds. No narrower controlling constitutional rationale can be extracted by treating their different reasons as interchangeable.

**Other limits:** No express waiver, automatic reciprocal tribal/state consent, constructive waiver by negotiating, or delegation of the United States' immunity exemption establishes this suit; the United States is an amicus. The Court does not reach the distinct Tenth Amendment defense first raised on appeal and not decided below. The question-scope limitation is prudential: actual X-Citement Video permits an appropriate respondent defense without requiring resolution of this distinct constitutional issue. No universal forfeiture rule, jurisdictional incapacity or independent mediator-appointments invalidation is announced.

**Precedent treatment.**

- **Ex parte Young:** Applied to this connected officer and ongoing federal statutory duty. The recognized route carries IGRA's limits and establishes no universal rule that detailed statutes preserve officer equity.
- **Edelman:** Its prospective/retrospective boundary remains. An injunction cannot be used to obtain accrued treasury compensation; prospective compliance costs alone do not decide that classification.
- **Pennhurst:** Its restriction on federal orders enforcing state law remains. Incorporation of state gaming law as part of the federal IGRA obligation does not itself turn this action into a state-law enforcement claim.
- **Union Gas:** Not overruled. Its actual damages judgment, statutory holding and five-vote constitutional conclusion remain precedent within their decided scope. The fractured rationale neither erases that conclusion nor makes every plurality sentence binding. Four Justices would overrule the constitutional conclusion; their dissent changes no law. Three unused constitutional alternatives cannot be aggregated with two affirmative State votes to create a present holding.
- **Hans:** Not overruled. The separate common-law accounts of its nontextual immunity do not become a Court holding, and the State set-aside does not abolish its rule.
- **Fitzpatrick:** Its distinct Fourteenth Amendment authority is unaffected; the decision establishes no new Reconstruction ground.
- **Aetna Life Insurance Co. v. Haworth, 300 U.S. 227:** Applied for the judicial character of specific, conclusive declaratory relief in an actual dispute over present rights. The declaratory statute is procedural; it creates neither a constitutional controversy nor an otherwise missing substantive action. The absence of a damages or injunction award is not alone disqualifying.
- **Nashville, Chattanooga & St. Louis Railway v. Wallace, 288 U.S. 249:** Applied for the proposition that an adverse, conclusive declaratory adjudication can be judicial without execution or coercive process. Its actual state-tax controversy does not establish that a declaratory label alone supplies legal effect or an IGRA remedy.
- **ICC v. Brimson, 154 U.S. 447:** Applied as support for judicial adjudication assisting administration, while preserving its ordinary adversarial proceeding, conclusive judgment and judicially enforceable order. Contempt there followed disobedience of the court's order, not merely the agency's request. It neither establishes an IGRA contempt remedy nor alone answers whether a differently structured intermediate judgment is judicial.
- **United States v. Ferreira, 54 U.S. 40:** Distinguished. The judge acted as a claims commissioner in a process lacking ordinary suit, parties, process and court record; no debt arose without Treasury approval, and the Secretary could revise the award. IGRA's conclusive adjudication and prescribed legal consequences differ. Ferreira's reserved appointments question supplies no mediator ruling; the appended Yale Todd account is a later inferential report, not a recorded reasoned holding.
- **Gordon v. United States, 69 U.S. 561, and the later appendix at 117 U.S. 697:** The actual disposition dismissed for want of appellate jurisdiction without a contemporaneous reasoned opinion. Taney's prepared paper, considered after his death and later printed, was not a delivered majority opinion; the contemplated Court opinion was never prepared. Its execution language informs the historical concern about legal effect contingent on another branch, but is not an unqualified holding requiring execution in every judicial case.
- **Hayburn's Case, 2 U.S. 409:** The reported Supreme Court proceeding produced no merits decision. The circuit judges' communications printed in the note explain objections to executive suspension and legislative revision of purported judicial decisions. They remain relevant historical materials, not a reasoned Supreme Court holding deciding IGRA's constrained later process.
- **Wisconsin v. City of New York:** Its concrete partial-redress holding supplies a limited analogy. It did not decide whether IGRA assigns a judicial function, eliminate Stevens's doubt or guarantee the claimant's preferred ultimate result.
- **Morgan Stanley/Plaut:** Its protection of the completed, unappealed private securities judgment remains confined to that actual holding. It supplies no universal answer to judicial character, executive implementation or finality under this different statute.
- **Puerto Rico Aqueduct:** Applied to the immediate appeal of the conclusive immunity denial. Appealability resolves neither immunity nor waiver, abrogation or the officer route's merits.
- **Hess:** Its entity-specific arm-of-State analysis does not resolve Florida's own immunity or congressional abrogation.
- **Hafer:** Its personal-capacity damages holding remains separate from the official-capacity prospective action recognized here.
- **New York v. United States:** Its compulsory regulation-or-ownership rule and distinct permitted inducements remain effective. It does not resolve the separate Tenth Amendment defense left unadjudicated here.
- **Voting Rights Coalition:** Its election-power grounds and United States enforcement posture supply no general Indian Commerce abrogation or state-command rule.
- **X-Citement Video:** Its allowance for an appropriate prevailing-respondent defense is preserved without compelling adjudication of this distinct Tenth Amendment issue. The Court's question-scope limit remains prudential.

**Law after decision.**

From March 27, 1996, the controlling rules reject the categorical advisory-function objection to this legally effective IGRA adjudication and permit the connected prospective officer action within the complete statutory sequence. No general rule that every detailed scheme preserves or excludes Young is adopted. Six actual writers agree that IGRA clearly authorizes a State action, but the judgment creates no controlling rule on Congress's power to subject Florida to that action.

The State-removal judgment binds the parties without a controlling State-amenability rationale. Union Gas remains precedent; the decision neither adopts a general Article I abrogation power nor establishes the dissent's general Article I prohibition. Statutory duty, cause, defendant, constitutional power, merits and remedy remain separate. The judgment supplies no direct-State jurisdiction by default, Secretary bypass, new damages action or gaming authorization.

**Procedure after action.**

The case returns for proceedings consistent with the officer holding, shared State set-aside and preserved statutory conditions. The separate September 22, 1993 merits judgment and stayed appeal No. 93-5256 require their own lawful treatment; this decision supplies neither reversal of that judgment nor a finding of bad faith. The State claim remains unterminated by the immunity disposition, with no majority determination of State amenability and no mandatory avoidance sequence imposed by the Court.

No immediate compacting order, mediator appointment, default proposal, Secretarial prescription, damages, game-scope declaration or license issues from this decision. The distinct asserted Secretary substitute remedy, independent administrative authority, complete state-law compacting authority, Tenth Amendment question and mediator-appointments issue remain unadjudicated. No special mandate date or continuing Supreme Court supervision is ordered.

Authority: [Public decision](../records/Seminole_Tribe_of_Florida_v_Florida_merits_1996-03-27.md).

### OCC national-bank interest rule — April 1, 1996

**Effective source; no judicial holding.** Published February 9, 1996, effective April 1, 1996. Exact Law After Decision from the bounded [public source](../entering-law/PUBLIC_OCC_national_bank_interest_rule_7_4001_regulatory_effectiveness_1996-04-01.md):

Section 7.4001(a) defines §85 interest to include payment compensating a creditor or prospective creditor for extending credit, making a credit line available, or a borrower's default or breach of a condition of credit. Its examples include numerical periodic rates, late fees, insufficient-funds fees, overlimit fees, annual fees, cash-advance fees and membership fees connected with credit extension or availability. It ordinarily excludes appraisal fees, insurance premiums and commissions guaranteeing repayment, finders' fees, document-preparation or notarization fees and credit-report fees.

Under (b), a national bank may charge the highest interest permitted to a home-state chartered or licensed lender, subject to home-state provisions material to the applicable loan class; the small-loan example retains loan-size restrictions without requiring the bank to obtain that state license. Under (c), the federal definition does not alter definitions or calculations used solely for state law. Home-state-permitted late fees may be charged interstate as federal interest even when home-state law excludes those fees from its own interest calculation. Under (d), a bank in a State denying corporate borrowers a usury defense may charge such a borrower the agreed interest rate.

These provisions take effect April 1, 1996. The instrument supplies no separate late-fee retroactivity or pending-case transition rule. Judicial treatment of the interpretation in a case involving earlier transactions and the validity of particular fees remain to be decided in the proper proceeding. Non-interest-charge rules are distinct from §7.4001.

No pending Court case changes stage by this entry. The regulation's treatment in a particular case depends on its subject matter, terms and the legal questions properly presented.

No judicial opinion or separate writing accompanies this source; it changes no precedent or assignment.

### O’Connor — April 1, 1996

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court, Parts I–III | O'Connor | Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | Reversal of the reviewed merits affirmance and bounded remand | Entire opinion. |
| Partial join in the Court opinion | — | Stone-Zsela | Same judgment and remedy | Parts I and III; Part II except its categorical proposition that an insignificant replacement-age difference, standing alone, does not support the necessary inference. His assent preserves that a minor difference or materially different circumstances may fail to support an inference. |

The general insignificance-alone proposition has eight direct votes. The other holdings and bounded judgment have nine at their stated scope. No separate opinion is filed, and no fractured-opinion synthesis is needed.

**Precedent treatment.**

- **McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792; Furnco Construction Corp. v. Waters, 438 U.S. 567; International Brotherhood of Teamsters v. United States, 431 U.S. 324:** Preserve the prima facie showing's function of supporting an inference; their factual formulations do not impose an under-40 replacement condition. General ADEA applicability remains assumed for this question.
- **Texas Department of Community Affairs v. Burdine, 450 U.S. 248, and Postal Service Board of Governors v. Aikens, 460 U.S. 711:** Preserve the distinction between an initial inference, employer production and ultimate employee persuasion concerning actual discrimination.
- **Hazen Paper Co. v. Biggins, 507 U.S. 604:** Applies its actual-age-motivation principle without requiring proof of the entire ultimate case at the initial stage. Its remaining causation and willfulness rules are unchanged.
- **St. Mary's Honor Center v. Hicks, 509 U.S. 502:** Preserves its rejection of compulsory liability after employer explanations are produced and disbelieved, and its rejection of a mandatory additional category of proof. No new persuasion allocation follows.
- **McKennon v. Nashville Banner Publishing Co., 513 U.S. 352:** Applies its separation of correction of an ADEA legal bar from proof of liability and lawful relief; its distinct after-acquired-evidence remedy is not extended here.
- **Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242, and Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317:** Preserve ordinary summary-judgment requirements and constrain further consideration without deciding the present evidence's ultimate sufficiency.

**Law after decision.**

The replacement's protected status is no longer a permissible categorical condition of the assumed ADEA prima facie formulation. Relative age must be assessed for its connection to prohibited discrimination; a substantially younger replacement may support the inference, while an insignificant difference alone is insufficient under the eight-Justice general rule. No numerical minimum or universally indispensable replacement element is created.

The plaintiff's ultimate persuasion obligation and the employer's opportunity to produce a lawful explanation remain. Correction of the age-40 condition guarantees neither trial nor recovery and does not reopen distinct unreviewed rulings. Specific small-gap applications, the effect of additional evidence and alternative formulations remain unresolved within the stated limits.

### Lonchar — April 1, 1996

**Judgment and remedy.**

| Component | Disposition and support | Supporting Justices | Opposing Justices | Immediate effect |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Appellate order vacating the district execution stay | Set aside and remanded, 9–0 as to operative relief; eight formally vacate and remand, while Stone-Zsela would reverse and remand | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer | None as to the common set-aside/remand | Removes the appellate order's displacement of the district stay; restores that stay pending prompt lawful redetermination, subject to modification or dissolution. |

Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer support the formal vacatur. Stone-Zsela's different verb does not represent opposition to the common relief or a substantive remedial dissent. No separate Supreme Court stay is issued. Restoring the displaced district order preserves the proceeding for the directed examination; it approves neither indefinite continuation nor protection throughout every future merits step. No new execution date or numerical stay period is fixed.

**Opinion topology.**

| Writing or component | Author | Joined by | Scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court, Parts I, II and IV | Stevens | Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer | All nine adopt the dismissal rule, distinct lawful stay inquiry and corrective remand. Part IV preserves Stone-Zsela's reversal formulation and the eight Associates' vacatur without changing their shared operative relief. |
| Opinion of the Court, Part III | Stevens | Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer | Five adopt protection necessary for genuinely identified statutory process when execution would defeat it and lawful prompt disposition cannot finish in time. Kennedy's assent is confined to that necessary opportunity, whose extent is not determined here. |

O'Connor, Scalia and Thomas reserve Part III's general proposition beyond the protection needed for this corrective remand. Stone-Zsela does not join Part III and supplies no separate position on its conditional rule. Their support for the remand is not a join in that additional explanation. No separate opinion is filed merely to restate those boundaries.

**Holdings and complete conditions.**

### I. Delay does not supply the asserted additional dismissal sanction

**Controlling proposition:** A first personal federal habeas petition satisfying the governing jurisdictional and pleading requirements may not be terminated solely for the reported delay and litigation purpose through an additional equitable sanction that dispenses with the conditions of the habeas statutes and Rules. Delay may support dismissal through Rule 9 or another lawful source only when that source's own predicates are satisfied.

**Authority:** Part I has all nine Justices' direct support.

**Controlling explanation:** Congress and the Habeas Rules allocate authority over initial examination, exhaustion, default, repeated applications, prejudicial delay and claims plainly lacking entitlement. Section 2243's direction to dispose of a matter as law and justice require operates within that arrangement; it does not authorize an additional terminal bar whenever a court regards a prisoner's timing or purpose as offensive.

Rule 9(a) specifically addresses delay prejudicing the State's ability to respond. Its reasonable-diligence qualification and Congress's deletion of a proposed five-year presumption would lose their work if generalized delay alone could replace them. The different predicates for repeated or abusive applications likewise cannot be supplied by counting unsuccessful next-friend captions.

The appellate opinion identifies serious conduct, not merely proximity to execution. Those findings retain significance under applicable law. But neither their seriousness nor the word “equity” establishes a Rule 9 condition, claim insufficiency or another lawful ground to extinguish this petition. The district court's refusal to employ that additional dismissal sanction was not the error the court of appeals supposed.

This conclusion preserves structured judicial judgment and source-authorized control of schedules, stays and sanctions. It excuses no deliberate misconduct, decides no unpresented fraud or inherent-power issue, and eliminates no established exhaustion, default or other claim-specific defense. It does not find that any undisclosed claim warrants relief.

**Statutory qualifications:**

- Pre-AEDPA §2254(a) requires custody violating federal law. Sections (b)–(c) retain exhaustion, including the absence or ineffectiveness of available state corrective process; an available state procedure cannot simply be disregarded. The then-effective factual-presumption provisions remain distinct from any later statutory deference regime.
- Section 2243's initial writ-or-show-cause command has an exception when the application shows nonentitlement. Its law-and-justice direction does not guarantee a writ or evidentiary hearing. Rule 4 requires prompt examination, summary dismissal and notice if lack of entitlement plainly appears from the petition and exhibits, and otherwise an answer or other appropriate judicial action, with service on the respondent and state attorney general. Lawful expedition remains available.
- Rule 9(a) permits dismissal for filing delay that prejudiced the State's ability to respond, unless the petitioner shows that reasonable diligence could not have disclosed the grounds before the prejudice arose. Losing an execution date or bearing generalized finality costs does not alone establish that response prejudice. The enacted Rule contains **no five-year presumption**; the deleted proposal in older advisory discussion is not law.
- Rule 9(b) separately concerns second or successive petitions: no new or different grounds after a prior merits determination, or new or different grounds whose earlier omission constituted abuse. Prior proceedings must be examined for their actual disposition, not merely counted.
- Section 2244(b)'s then-effective subsequent-application permission follows a federal denial of habeas relief after an evidentiary hearing on a material factual merits issue or a hearing on a legal merits issue. Its exception requires both an unadjudicated factual or other ground and absence of deliberate withholding or other abuse. New evidence is not automatically a new ground; absence of withholding does not eliminate every other abuse. When both conditions are met and other barriers are absent, McCleskey requires consideration. The State must plead abuse clearly and particularly before the prisoner's burden arises. No such subsequent-petition predicate is established here.

### II. Independent equitable stay discretion survives the dismissal ruling

**Controlling proposition:** First-petition status does not exclude lawful independent consideration of the State's enforcement interest, unjustified delay or proved obstruction in deciding an execution stay. But the existence of that distinct discretion does not sustain this appellate order, whose stated premise was the supposed authority to dismiss through the sanction rejected in Part I.

**Authority:** Part II has all nine Justices' direct support.

**Controlling explanation:** Gomez permits equitable assessment independently of a habeas procedural bar, even on an assumed open procedural route. Its four earlier petitions are facts of that case, not a minimum number needed before equity may operate. The State therefore presents a genuine stay argument, and its reported conduct findings cannot be dismissed as irrelevant merely because this is Lonchar's first personal petition.

McFarland likewise preserves denial for proved inexcusable disregard of a reasonable statutory opportunity and obstruction, while protecting that opportunity. The seriousness of a supported constitutional claim and execution's irreversibility matter without alone compelling last-minute relief. Neither case licenses an unsourced permanent dismissal or establishes what examination this actual petition has received.

The appellate order treats supposed dismissal authority as the reason the district court erred in granting a stay. Once that legal premise is removed, the reported conduct does not itself supply a separate determination that all required process occurred or that a lawful claim-specific disposition is available. Corrective remand allows the courts below to evaluate those questions and genuine independent stay grounds on the proper basis. It does not forbid sustaining a stay refusal on an adequately established independent ground.

**Section 2251 limits:** A federal justice or judge before whom a habeas proceeding is pending **may** stay covered State proceedings before final judgment, after final judgment **of discharge**, or pending appeal. The covered matter must involve the detained person and a matter involved in the habeas proceeding. Proceedings within a granted stay are void; without a stay, they remain as valid as if no habeas proceeding or appeal were pending. Filing alone therefore supplies no suspension, and the statute does not invalidate unrelated State action. Its discretionary text does not by itself answer whether protection is necessary for an otherwise required judicial opportunity.

### III. Protection must preserve genuinely required process when lawful expedition cannot

**Controlling proposition:** If execution would prevent completion of process actually required by the governing habeas statute and Rules, and lawful prompt disposition cannot finish in time, a court must provide the interim protection necessary to make that identified opportunity meaningful. Mere filing, first-petition status or a capital sentence establishes neither condition.

**Authority:** Part III has five direct supporters: Stevens, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer. Kennedy joins only the necessary-opportunity formulation, without resolving the opportunity's extent on this record. O'Connor, Scalia and Thomas reserve the general proposition; Stone-Zsela supplies no additional join.

**Controlling explanation:** Barefoot protects meaningful review in its specified initial-appeal setting. Its reasoning supports, by analogy, protection for whatever examination the first-petition statute and Rules actually require. This is an extension of that meaningful-review principle to a different stage, not direct application of a certificate-of-probable-cause rule whose trigger has not been established here. McFarland reinforces protection of a real statutory opportunity while retaining individualized limits for established disregard and obstruction.

The court must identify what process remains due. Rule 4 screening, lawful procedural dismissal, appropriate expedition and the absence of an automatic evidentiary hearing remain effective. If those means permit a lawful disposition in time, this conditional rule supplies no further stay entitlement. Nor does it erase the actual opportunity and obstruction inquiry in McFarland or the independent equitable considerations preserved in Gomez.

Execution cannot replace process that governing law still requires merely because the court lacks time to perform it. Necessary protection makes that legal obligation effective; it does not guarantee every requested merits step. The present decision finds neither that a particular undisclosed claim requires further review nor that a particular period is necessary. Those are matters for the directed examination and reasoned stay redetermination.

**Barefoot's distinct settings remain intact:**

- A first district petition receives no automatic suspension upon filing. The rule above identifies an analogy and requires its own actual-process and timing predicates.
- On an **initial habeas appeal with a certificate of probable cause**, meaningful opportunity to address the merits and an appellate merits decision are required. If execution would moot review and time prevents a considered disposition, a stay must issue. Adequate notice and opportunity to address the merits permit expedited or simultaneous merits/stay decision. Certification requires more than nonfrivolity: a substantial federal showing, including reasonably debatable issues, possible different resolution or questions deserving further consideration; neither ultimate success nor sentence severity alone is the test. No final denial and certified appeal are established here.
- Second or successive petitions retain Rule 9(b)'s actual conditions, lawful expedition and the requirement that a stay reflect substantial grounds upon which relief might be granted. Failed next-friend proceedings do not alone put this petition in that setting.
- Pending certiorari after appellate habeas denial, a stay is not automatic. There must be a reasonable probability that four Members would find the issue sufficiently meritorious for certiorari or notation of probable jurisdiction, a significant possibility of reversal and likely irreparable harm. The application must supply materials for careful assessment; relief should first be sought in the court of appeals, whose action generally receives considerable weight in that setting. These are not the merits criteria for this already-argued challenge.

### IV. This legal error requires corrective remand and prompt stay redetermination

**Controlling proposition:** The appellate stay-vacatur judgment cannot stand on its erroneous dismissal premise. Remand proceeds through the Eleventh Circuit for prompt district examination of the actual petition and proper State objections and redetermination of the need and terms of §2251 protection. Removing the appellate order restores the displaced district stay pending that decision, subject to lawful modification or dissolution.

**Authority:** All nine support this operative correction. The eight Associates formally vacate and remand; Stone-Zsela would reverse and remand. All support the limited restoration independently of any additional Part III join.

**Controlling explanation:** The order under review displaced an existing district stay on a mistaken legal understanding. Setting it aside restores the prior protection so the directed examination can occur, while requiring the courts below promptly to apply the correct law. That consequence differs from issuing a new Supreme Court stay or declaring every first petitioner entitled to continued protection.

The reported conduct findings remain available for lawful assessment. They do not establish Rule 9 prejudice, procedural default, nonexhaustion, abuse, claim insubstantiality or completion of all required examination. The Court supplies none of those missing determinations. Nor does it direct a hearing or full constitutional-merits adjudication despite lawful barriers. Once the required examination permits lawful disposition or establishes that protection is unnecessary, this mandate supplies no entitlement to further delay. The existing order may be modified or dissolved consistently with the governing law; indefinite continuation is not approved.

**Precedent treatment.**

- **Gomez:** Retained as an independent equitable stay rule, not reduced to successive-abuse doctrine. Its assumed open procedural route and record-specific balancing remain material; four earlier petitions are not a minimum trigger. It creates neither the asserted additional first-petition dismissal ground nor an automatic late-claim bar.
- **McFarland:** Applied for a meaningful statutory opportunity and individualized stay discretion, including denial for proved inexcusable disregard and obstruction. Its qualified counsel/preparation proceeding and preapplication pendency holding do not establish Lonchar's preparation facts or an unconditional stay. An actual application is present here.
- **Barefoot:** Part III extends its meaningful-review reasoning by analogy to genuinely required district process. Its initial-appeal/CPC, successive-petition and certiorari formulations remain confined to their respective triggers and qualifications stated above. No certified appeal is invented, and lawful expedition is preserved.
- **Schlup:** Its legal-error remand supports correcting the asserted mistaken premise without predetermining further proceedings or relief. Its crime-innocence gateway still requires reliable evidence and the probative record as a whole to show that it is more likely than not that no reasonable, properly instructed juror would convict. Reliability, likely credibility, delay and inconsistency matter; mere possibility, ordinary merits prejudice or a reviewing judge's doubt does not suffice. No gateway is found satisfied here, and innocence is not an entry requirement for every first petition.
- **Sawyer:** Its separate death-eligibility gateway requires clear and convincing proof that, absent constitutional error, no reasonable juror would find eligibility under applicable state law. Additional discretionary mitigation does not satisfy it. It supplies no finding or universal first-petition condition here.
- **McCleskey:** Its abuse rules and clear, particular State pleading requirement remain within their actual habeas setting. The then-effective §2244(b) conditions are preserved rather than replaced by a generalized delay sanction.
- **Delo v. Stokes:** Its abuse-of-discretion review and successive-petition application retain their established scope. They do not by themselves establish an abuse ground or the merits-screening standard for this first personal petition.

No precedent is overruled. The judgment preserves source-authorized equity while rejecting the additional terminal sanction asserted below.

**Law after decision.**

From April 1, 1996, a first personal federal petition cannot be extinguished solely by the described delay and litigation purpose through an additional equitable dismissal rule dispensing with statutory and Habeas Rules conditions. Independent stay equity survives. Five Justices also establish the conditional protection needed for genuinely required process when execution would defeat it and lawful prompt disposition cannot finish in time.

These rules do not guarantee a stay, hearing, full merits proceedings or relief. Exhaustion, default, Rule 4, Rule 9, the then-effective subsequent-application rules, lawful expedition and source-authorized sanctions remain. No five-year delay presumption, later habeas regime, new innocence gateway or numerical timetable is created. The required corrective remand establishes no claim-specific factual predicate.

**Procedure after action.**

The appellate judgment vacating the district stay is removed. The displaced district stay is restored pending prompt redetermination under the correct legal framework, subject to lawful modification or dissolution. The case returns through the Eleventh Circuit to the District Court for examination of the actual petition and proper State objections, and a reasoned determination of any further protection needed under §2251.

No completed petition dismissal is reversed, no writ or evidentiary hearing is ordered, and no constitutional claim, innocence gateway, procedural bar, response prejudice or actual stay duration is resolved. The reported earlier execution setting supplies no present date. No separate Supreme Court execution stay, numerical period, indefinite continuation or continuing Supreme Court supervision is ordered.

Authority: [Public decision](../records/Lonchar_v_Thomas_merits_1996-04-01.md).

### Shieh and companions — April 1, 1996

**Judgment and remedy.**

All nine Justices—Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer—support each financial grant, each present-paper refusal and the separate prospective refusal.

| Matter | Financial motion | Present Rule 39.8 determination | Consequence |
|---|---|---|---|
| No. 95-7587, Kakita | Granted, 9–0, on its January 19 declaration | Proposed denial declined, 9–0, on this petition's notice/reopening showing | Individual filing without prepayment; certiorari pending. |
| No. 95-7588, Ninth Circuit | Granted, 9–0, on its separate January 22 declaration | Proposed denial declined, 9–0, on this petition's show-cause/notice showing | Individual filing without prepayment; certiorari pending. |
| No. 95-7589, Krieger | Granted, 9–0, on its separately reproduced January 19 declaration | Proposed denial declined, 9–0, on its own nonservice/reopening showing | Individual filing without prepayment; certiorari pending. |
| Future noncriminal certiorari petitions | No blanket financial determination | New fee-and-form condition declined, 9–0 | Future submissions remain subject to ordinary rules and governing law. |

No entity receives derivative financial relief. No payment or booklet-conversion condition, deadline, certiorari disposition, underlying relief or alteration of an existing lawful restriction follows. No petition poll is announced.

**Opinion topology.**

Justice Ginsburg delivers the Opinion of the Court, Parts I, II-A, II-B, II-C and III, joined throughout by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Breyer. Each controlling holding below has these nine direct joins.

Chief Justice Stone-Zsela also concurs separately, joined by no other Justice, proposing a stronger presumption against predictive personal exclusions while joining the Court's bounded grounds. His additional principle is not a holding of the Court.

**Holdings and complete conditions.**

### I. Each individual financial submission supports leave

**Holding:** L. Shieh's separately signed declarations establish financial eligibility for each of the three motions on this record. The grants rest on each application's actual showing and create neither an irrebuttable-affidavit rule nor derivative relief for the corporation appearing in two captions.

**Authority:** Part I, joined by all nine Justices.

**Controlling explanation:** Rule 39.1 requires the prescribed motion identifying other-court financial applications and their dispositions, with a Form 4 notarized affidavit or §1746 declaration. Its exception for counsel appointed by a United States district or appellate court under the Criminal Justice Act or another applicable federal statute requires citation of that statute; no exception is invoked here.

Each dated declaration reports no current employment, no income during its own preceding twelve months, no cash/accounts or listed valuable property, and former April 1989 employment at approximately $7,500 gross monthly. Former earnings are not present resources. The blank dependents line claims no dependent expense but does not negate those answers; the separate California fee grant does not control this Court.

The August 1995 English document appended to each petition describes annual gross income often reaching several million dollars. That recent statement supplies a substantial reason to consider clarification for each motion. It identifies no dated receipts during the reporting periods or presently available funds or assets, however, and its alleged interruption of client representation prevents treating it as an unambiguous disclosure of accessible wealth. The later specific sworn answers adequately address the relevant questions here. The Court neither authenticates that document nor finds its account false.

Attwood supports an adequately established individual showing; Jones's reservation arose from unestablished financial particulars, unlike the declarations before the Court. Particular further inquiry remains permissible when needed. Under Rowland, an entity may seek relief through its own authorized actual-means showing, with lawful representation still required; Shieh's declarations decide no entity application. These financial grants alone establish no entitlement to certiorari or relief.

### II-A. Kakita's particular notice and reopening objection is not disposed of by its other defects

**Holding:** The present showing does not establish a basis for the proposed Rule 39.8 denial in No. 95-7587. This refusal depends on the particular petition's identified nonservice/reopening contention, not on immunity for its broader allegations.

**Authority:** Part II-A, joined by all nine Justices.

**Controlling explanation:** Rule 39.8 permits, but does not require, denial when the Court is satisfied that the particular covered filing is frivolous or malicious. Zatko preserves supported denials; Martin distinguishes arguable current content from combined sufficient defects. Denton's factual screen does not permit ordinary disbelief to resolve genuine disputes and does not itself supply the complete Rule 39.8 standard.

Kakita's no-review and complete-ban accounts conflict with the October 27 order, which recites review of the opening brief and record and bars additional submissions in the identified closed dockets. The appeal concerns denials of reopening, not unrestricted direct review. The foreign-criminal and misconduct assertions establish no underlying facts.

This petition nevertheless identifies an allegedly unserved summary-judgment motion and district order and connects that nonservice to reopening. The review recital and closed-docket direction do not answer that specific contention. Missing underlying papers establish neither service failure or preserved error nor a conclusive independent defeat of the objection. Martin, Anderson, Attwood and Jones require that particular assessment. Merely using notice language would not protect an otherwise demonstrated frivolous filing; the identified motion, order and asserted reopening ground matter here. No independent malice finding supplies a denial ground. The Court finds neither unlawful procedure nor entitlement to review.

### II-B. The separate challenge to the prospective appellate order presents its own notice question

**Holding:** The Court declines the proposed Rule 39.8 denial in No. 95-7588 on the present showing. The petition's concrete show-cause and notice contention is not resolved by the visible order's retained filing routes or recital of an opportunity to respond.

**Authority:** Part II-B, joined by all nine Justices.

**Controlling explanation:** This petition alleges nonreceipt in Taiwan of the October 27 show-cause order, challenges the fourteen-day response period and documents a January 17 request for the missing paper before the January 22 petition. The fax evidence establishes the request, not failed mailing or the truth of the alleged telephone account.

The December 13 order recites show cause and failure to respond. Its visible paragraph (1) excludes counsel-represented and district-certified nonfrivolous appeals from the pro se notice-of-appeal restriction. Paragraph (5) permits a reasoned lifting request no earlier than January 1, 1998, and continues the order until further order. These qualifications contradict an absolute-ban account; they do not establish the adequacy of notice. The missing middle page and absent original show-cause/service materials also prevent a complete account of the permission procedure.

Anderson, Attwood and Jones require assessing the particular procedural issue apart from the broad allegations. The established adverse features do not dispose of it sufficiently to support the proposed denial. This ruling adopts no actual-receipt requirement, general fourteen-day rule or finding that the restriction is unlawful. Rule 39.8 remains available upon its particular showing; the Court neither validates the petition's other theories nor grants certiorari.

### II-C. Krieger's own nonservice claim must be assessed within its reopening posture

**Holding:** The Court declines the proposed Rule 39.8 denial in No. 95-7589 on the present showing. Krieger's identified nonservice and reopening argument requires its own assessment, independently of Kakita and the different show-cause claim in No. 95-7588.

**Authority:** Part II-C, joined by all nine Justices.

**Controlling explanation:** The actual appellate ruling concerns denial of reopening, so the petition's de novo summary-judgment theories do not enlarge the review available. Its foreign-proceeding, treaty, discovery, preclusion and amendment assertions establish no entitlement. The no-new-arguments ruling and exaggerated allegations are substantial grounds to scrutinize this petition.

But its own body alleges nonservice of the summary-judgment motion and district order and invokes Rule 60(b)(6) and Molloy as grounds for reopening. The October 27 order cites Molloy for abuse-of-discretion review and Backlund for refusing vacatur when no new arguments are raised. Those references do not themselves establish a conclusive answer to the identified notice ground. The March 3 order records denials of reconsideration, discovery and amendment, not the missing papers' contents or service facts.

As Martin, Anderson, Attwood and Jones require, the Court separates this concrete contention from defects elsewhere. Citation of Rule 60 alone would not establish arguability; its connection to the identified allegedly unserved papers supplies the distinction here. The Court accepts neither the nonservice allegation nor Shieh's proposed legal construction, and announces no treaty, discovery, amendment or foreign-proceeding entitlement. No established malice independently supports denial. Financial access remains distinct from certiorari and underlying relief.

### III. The future condition lacks its separate supporting showing

**Holding:** A prospective condition on future noncriminal certiorari petitions requires support tied to the applicant, the relevant category and the inadequacy of treating particular submissions. The proposed new fee-and-form condition lacks that showing on this record and is declined.

**Authority:** Part III, joined by all nine Justices. The Court does not adopt the concurrence's additional strong presumption.

**Controlling explanation:** Martin, Day, Sassower, Anderson, Attwood and Jones require a distinct prospective inquiry. Lower restrictions and repeated litigation warrant scrutiny, but do not themselves establish abuse of this Court's relevant category or why individual treatment is inadequate. The present record establishes no sequence of this Court's earlier Shieh denials, warnings or failed limited responses that supplies the missing connection. That is a limit of the record, not a universal warning prerequisite.

Retaining paid and criminal routes narrows the proposal but does not justify it. Screening consumes real resources, and a properly supported targeted condition remains lawful under McDonald and Sindram within their distinct settings. Every conceivable lesser measure need not first fail. Here the necessary applicant/category/inadequacy showing remains absent, while the current papers illustrate why their particular procedural content requires assessment.

The Court imposes no numerical threshold, categorical immunity or new rule for extraordinary writs or habeas. It vacates no existing lawful restriction and preserves ordinary neutral filing requirements, valid finality and jurisdictional rules, and sanctions for proved misconduct.

**Precedent treatment.**

- **Zatko v. California:** Preserves supported denial of a particular frivolous or malicious filing; identity and earlier losses do not establish the necessary present defect.
- **Martin v. District of Columbia:** Applies its distinction between particular current papers and its separate prospective-control inquiry; the different current-paper outcomes remain meaningful.
- **Denton v. Hernandez, 504 U.S. 25:** Preserves the clearly-baseless factual threshold and prohibition on resolving genuine disputes through ordinary disbelief. Its district-court statutory screen is not treated as the complete Rule 39.8 test.
- **Rowland v. California Men's Colony, 506 U.S. 194:** Preserves an entity's own authorized actual-means showing and lawful-representation requirements; personal financial leave does not resolve corporate eligibility or means.
- **Day, Sassower and In re Anderson:** Apply their current-paper and applicant-specific, category-specific prospective limits without creating a universal warning or exhaustion rule.
- **Attwood v. Singletary, 516 U.S. 297:** Applies its adequate financial-showing, particular-access-content and separate prospective-ground distinctions. Its certiorari denial is not extended to these petitions.
- **Jones v. ABC-TV, 516 U.S. 363:** Applies the same separate inquiries while distinguishing its unestablished financial particulars from Shieh's three supported declarations. Its pending financial treatment is not a rule requiring reservation here.
- **In re McDonald, 489 U.S. 180, and In re Sindram, 498 U.S. 177:** Preserve bounded authority for properly supported targeted controls; they do not supply missing predicates for this proposal.

**Law after decision.**

Financial eligibility, present-paper screening, future filing controls and certiorari remain separate inquiries. The Court applies existing law to three individually supported financial motions and three distinct procedural contentions. It grants neither blanket future eligibility nor derivative entity relief, and finds neither the underlying allegations nor notice violations proved.

No new future noncriminal-certiorari condition issues on this record. Supported Rule 39.8 denials and properly justified targeted controls remain available. The concurrence's stronger presumption is noncontrolling, and all three petitions await separate consideration.

**Procedure after action.**

L. Shieh's three individual petitions proceed without prepayment and remain pending for their ordinary independent consideration. The order supplies no fee payment, Rule 33.1 conversion, deadline, noncompliance default, response order, hearing, counsel appointment or new filing restriction. Existing ordinary requirements concerning timeliness, service, form, jurisdiction and substance remain applicable. No underlying judgment or existing lawful restriction is set aside.

Authority: [Public decision](../records/Shieh_and_companions_filing_order_1996-04-01.md).

### Bowersox — interim application order — April 9, 1996

**Event.**

Bowersox v. Williams, application No. A-828; 517 U.S. 345. October Term 1995. Interim order, April 9, 1996, on Missouri's application to vacate an Eighth Circuit execution stay concerning Doyle J. Williams.

The third federal petition was denied January 11, following adoption of Magistrate Judge Hays's report; amendment was also denied. A certificate of probable cause issued. The March 8 appellate stay extends through submission and further appellate order, with argument scheduled May 13. Execution had been scheduled for April 10. No exact execution hour is established here. The available account describes a summary appellate order without articulated reasons.

**Participation.**

The application is presented to Justice O'Connor, the Eighth Circuit Justice, and by her referred to the Court. Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer participate.

**Public Action.**

Final disposition of the application is reserved for immediate examination of the actual application record. The Court orders:

1. The Clerk shall promptly circulate the application, any response and relevant papers already filed, and promptly transmit this order to counsel by appropriately speedy means.
2. Counsel shall immediately identify the operative appellate stay and later orders, the exact execution setting if known, and the grounds on which the challenged stay is defended or attacked. To the extent not already lodged and identified in this Court's file, they shall furnish the third petition, pertinent earlier dispositions, the magistrate report and objections, the January 11 ruling, proposed amendment and denial, and certificate and scope. Only papers material to the asserted grounds are required. Existing filings may satisfy this direction by identification; duplicative filing and an unrelated complete trial record are not required.
3. Initial supplementation shall conclude **two hours after the Clerk's prompt transmission**. Within that period counsel may identify a particular unavailable paper, explain its materiality and request an adjustment. Each side may promptly answer new material. Inability to produce or silence establishes no concession, abuse or insubstantiality; ultimate burdens remain unchanged.
4. The procedural reservation ends upon completion of immediate review or **four hours after transmission, whichever occurs first**. The still-pending application shall then return to the Court for immediate determination of the next lawful action. It shall return earlier when execution circumstances or completed submissions warrant. No automatic continuation follows; further judicial delay requires a separately supported action.
5. **No new Supreme Court execution stay issues.** This order neither enlarges, shortens nor finally approves the existing appellate stay. Expiration of the processing interval does not dissolve that stay, authorize execution, deny the application or adjudicate a habeas claim. The appellate stay remains governed by its own terms unless lawfully modified.

**Judgment & Remedy.**

| Component | Support and opposition | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Reserve final disposition for immediate examination of the actual record | All nine support: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer | No final grant or denial of Missouri's application. |
| Exact party-directed supplementation and transmission-based processing procedure above | Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer adopt it; Stone-Zsela retains his different proposed mechanism | Two-hour supplementation and a maximum four-hour reservation, with earlier return as specified. |
| Issue no additional Supreme Court execution stay in this action | Eight Associates support; Stone-Zsela would add the administrative protection described in his statement | The existing appellate restraint is unaffected; no separate Supreme Court execution restraint is entered. |

Stone-Zsela agrees with the common reservation and record examination but does not adopt the complete operative order. His nonjoin does not announce opposition to every provision allowing earlier review. None of the nine takes a final grant-or-deny position on the State's application in this action.

**Opinion Topology.**

Justice Kennedy delivers the Court's explanation, Parts I–III. Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer join throughout. Chief Justice Stone-Zsela joins Part I only and files a signed statement concurring in part and dissenting in part on the proposed record mechanism and additional execution protection.

Part I has nine direct supporters. Parts II–III have eight. The signed adoptions below refer to these identified parts; no agreement on final vacatur or a habeas claim is inferred.

**Holdings.**

### I. Final disposition is reserved for immediate record examination

**Controlling proposition:** The Court reserves the State's application while immediately obtaining and examining the actual basis needed to decide it. This is an interim procedural action, not a determination that the appellate stay is lawful or unlawful or that any habeas ground warrants relief.

**Authority:** Kennedy's Part I, joined by all nine Justices.

**Controlling explanation:** A decision whether to disturb this execution stay requires the actual grounds and relevant procedural posture. The petition's number, a certificate and a scheduled argument do not identify those grounds. Nor does an unexplained appellate order establish their absence. Immediate examination separates the information needed for decision from the decision itself.

Delo v. Blair's equal division provides no controlling rationale. McFarland's preparation opportunity and Schlup's gateway require their own predicates. Lonchar does not establish a Williams claim, an unmet procedural obligation or a necessary interval of execution protection. The Court therefore makes no final substantial-ground finding and selects no eventual result. The parties' actual papers, existing judicial grounds and material remaining questions must determine the next action.

### II. Application management supports the specified short processing order

**Controlling proposition:** For this pending referred application, the Court directs circulation of existing papers and conditional supplementation of actually absent material on the two-hour/four-hour terms stated in the order. The deadlines regulate initial application processing and create no entitlement to a minimum delay or further habeas proceedings.

**Authority:** Kennedy's Part II, joined by Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. Stone-Zsela does not join this exact implementation.

**Controlling explanation:** Rule 22 governs the pending application and its referral. The Court may obtain the information necessary to consider that application; Barefoot's account of the Garrison submissions illustrates resolving an actual uncertainty about prior consideration through the papers. That procedural use grants no substantive habeas relief.

The order begins with what is already filed. A gap in an available source collection proves no omission from the Court's file, failure of service or failure of lower-court examination. Existing papers may permit immediate return without supplementation. Only actually absent, material documents require production, with an opportunity to identify an unavailable item and address new material.

The short maximum requires prompt attention to the State's request while permitting that examination. Two and four hours are this order's case-management terms, not periods prescribed by precedent. The four-hour endpoint returns the application for the next lawful decision; it guarantees neither adequate time for every merits inquiry nor any substantive result. The general motion-response period in Rule 21.4 does not apply simply because a Rule 22 application reaches the Court. Further Court-directed delay requires its own grounds and action.

### III. This processing order grants no additional execution protection

**Controlling proposition:** No independently established need for an additional Supreme Court execution stay supports the eight-Justice order on the present showing. The appellate restraint continues on its own terms, without new Supreme Court approval, shortening or extension.

**Authority:** Kennedy's Part III, joined by the seven other Associates. Stone-Zsela would grant the separate administrative protection stated below.

**Controlling explanation:** Missouri's pending application does not itself dissolve the appellate stay. Examination of that application can proceed under the existing restraint without treating unknown claims as substantial or finding a further habeas opportunity legally required. The need to determine the application therefore does not by itself establish a need for a second execution restraint.

A new administrative stay, a stay pending review and a final decision vacating an existing stay have different legal effects and require their respective grounds. The Court chooses none of those effects by setting a paper-processing interval. Rules 22–23 do not themselves manufacture substantive stay jurisdiction, and no new statutory injunction authority is decided. If later established circumstances require further action, its authority, basis, scope and ending event must be addressed then. The present order establishes no categorical prohibition on administrative protection and gives no permission to execute contrary to an operative stay.

**Precedent Treatment.**

- **Barefoot v. Estelle, 463 U.S. 880, and Delo v. Stokes, 495 U.S. 320:** The successive-petition stay standard requires substantial grounds upon which relief might be granted. Actual procedural availability, prior dispositions and any independent merits ground matter. Neither petition count nor appellate silence substitutes for that inquiry. Barefoot's meaningful-review and necessary-stay rules for an initial certified appeal retain that setting; a certificate in this successive proceeding is not an automatic stay entitlement. Its certiorari-stage probability and irreparable-harm test is separate. Stokes's separate All Writs and heightened-deference reasoning is not promoted into a Court holding.
- **Delo v. Blair:** The equal division supplies no Court precedent or majority rationale.
- **Gomez and McFarland:** Independent stay equity and the State's enforcement interest survive; serious claims and irreversibility do not alone compel late relief. McFarland protects its actual statutory preparation opportunity while preserving denial for proved inexcusable disregard and obstruction. No new preparation entitlement is established here.
- **Schlup and Sawyer:** Crime innocence and death-eligibility innocence retain different thresholds. Schlup requires reliable new evidence assessed with the whole probative record, showing that more likely than not no reasonable properly instructed juror would convict; mere possibility or a reviewing judge's doubt is insufficient. Sawyer requires clear and convincing proof that absent constitutional error no reasonable juror would find death eligibility under state law; added discretionary mitigation alone does not suffice. Neither gateway establishes an underlying violation or automatically grants relief or a stay. No gateway is found satisfied.
- **Lonchar:** Its first-personal-petition dismissal correction and conditional necessary-process protection do not displace the successive-petition rule. Any necessary-process application requires identifying the obligation still due and inability to complete it lawfully in time; those predicates are not established here. Its restoration of a displaced district stay supplies no automatic remedy in this case.

The pre-AEDPA statutes and Rules remain applicable. Rule 9(a) requires delay-caused prejudice to the State's ability to respond and preserves its reasonable-diligence qualification; there is no enacted five-year presumption. Rule 9(b) requires the actual prior-merits/repeated-ground or abuse predicates. The then-effective §2244(b) subsequent-application permission follows a federal denial after an evidentiary hearing on a material factual merits issue or a hearing on a legal merits issue. Its exception requires both an unadjudicated factual or other ground and absence of deliberate withholding or other abuse; the State's clear, particular abuse pleading precedes the prisoner's resulting burden. New evidence is not automatically a new ground. Exhaustion and its absence/ineffectiveness exceptions, default and independent merits grounds remain distinct. No current predicate is adjudicated.

The Court adds no new construction of §2251. No precedent is overruled and no final substantial-grounds standard is changed.

**Law After Decision.**

The order applies existing application-management authority to this pending request and fixes a short, conditional processing interval. It makes no change to the governing habeas, gateway or execution-stay standards and creates no automatic right to time for gathering every possible paper.

The State's application remains pending. The appellate stay retains its own force and terms; neither the two-hour supplementation limit nor the four-hour return point is an execution authorization or a new Supreme Court stay expiration.

**Procedure After Action.**

The Clerk is to circulate existing papers and transmit the order promptly. The two-hour supplementation and maximum four-hour procedural-reservation intervals run from actual transmission, whose time is not established here. Earlier completed review or execution circumstances require earlier return as specified. No service, completed supplementation or elapsed interval is presumed.

The still-pending application returns for immediate determination of the next lawful action on the actual papers and any identified material limitation. No final vacatur, denial, new execution stay, automatic extension, execution permission or protection through May 13 follows. Existing appellate protection remains governed by its own order unless lawfully modified. Any later Court action has its own grounds and date.

The foregoing order records the action of the Court. The participating Justices' positions and the reasons they adopt are set out above. **Certified for issuance: Chief Justice Alex-Lamar Stone-Zsela.**

**Source Notes.**

The available procedural account identifies the third petition, January 11 district action, magistrate report, amendment ruling, certificate, March 8 appellate stay, argument setting and planned execution date. It does not supply the actual claims, material prior dispositions, report and objections, district reasoning, amendment papers, certificate scope, complete appellate orders or the State's application and Williams's response. Their absence from the available collection establishes no omission from any court's file and supports no finding that either side withheld papers or conceded a ground.

The governing Rules are effective October 2, 1995. The retained official pre-AEDPA §§2243, 2251 and 2254 and Habeas Rules support the stated limits. Complete standalone official 1994 §§2253 and 1651 were not recovered; neither modern text nor a separate Justice's citation supplies an unverified independent statutory ground. Barefoot and Stokes supply their verified procedural and stay propositions. This interim order establishes no unknown claim, procedural default, abuse, exhaustion defect, gateway, service fact or actual execution hour.
