### Ayers v. Fordice — March 25, 1996

**Stone-Zsela, dissenting.** The Chief Justice would vacate only the additional-library-relief denial. When an established segregation-caused educational injury remains unremedied, the absence of predicted additional white enrollment cannot by itself justify refusing necessary, practicable and educationally sound repair. Fordice places the dismantlement burden on the State and requires examination of interacting inherited policies. Jenkins recognizes educational repair as an independently sufficient ground; Milliken II connects educational remedies beyond pupil assignment to the violation. Its application to university libraries develops the doctrine; Milliken II did not decide this question.

The district court attributed collection differences to historical missions and denied enlargement beyond them because the holdings were not shown to preclude the institutions as viable choices for white students. It also credited Jackson State and Alcorn expansions. The dissent preserves supported findings, including those about volume counts and student choice, but finds the educational-repair inquiry unresolved. Different lawful missions may require different collections. Inherited missions cannot conclusively justify resource limits when mission policies continue fostering separation and library allocations are traceable to the extent they follow those missions.

Reconsideration would ask whether a library condition attributable to the dual system remains unremedied, what resources are needed for each institution's legally justified mission—including the program changes already ordered in decree paragraphs 3–10—and what practicable, educationally sound repair remains necessary after crediting the existing improvements. Neither traceability, historical inadequacy nor a collection disparity itself establishes a present injury or a necessary expenditure. If the libraries adequately support lawful missions and existing improvements remedy any attributable injury, no additional relief follows.

The proposed remand preserves existing findings and leaves all other decree provisions and appellate challenges undisturbed without merits affirmance. It reopens no mission, program, admissions or equipment determination and adjudicates no scholarship or endowment eligibility, committee procedure, maintenance control or reporting deadline. It requires neither identical collections nor funding parity, a fixed appropriation, new hearing, universal proof protocol or withdrawal of supervision. Historically black institutions are not themselves the constitutional wrong. Any release question retains Freeman's and Jenkins's distinct requirements.

### Morse v. Republican Party of Virginia, No. 94-203; 517 U.S. 186 — March 27, 1996

**Stevens, concurring, joined throughout by Ginsburg.** They join the Court's limited application and both reversals but also adopt a broader functional explanation. Virginia recognizes the qualifying party's choice and certification as the means of obtaining preferential general-ballot access. That authority concerns an official stage of electoral choice; a monetary prerequisite to exercising it affects the effectiveness of voting under §§5 and 14. Allen, Sheffield and the White Primary Cases support coverage through delegated electoral authority, including the party-office/delegate route, without requiring that the nominee be virtually certain to win. The regulation's primary example is not exhaustive, and the statute itself supplies authority without administrative deference creating a missing power.

Their rule still requires an electoral function and a change affecting voting; it does not cover all party activity. They reject the asserted association obstacle to submission of this fee without approving every hypothetical application. Hurley preserves actual expressive choice, while the fee duty compels neither a message nor a candidate. They retain the pleading-versus-proof and nomination-method reservations and adopt the Court's Act-specific §10 ground without a poll-tax or refund finding.

They additionally conclude that the recurring fee practice, the Party's continued defense without disavowal and the unreturned payment preserve this controversy, including as capable of repetition yet evading review. That case-specific ground does not establish that every election dispute remains live or that every prospective request here is available. Their broader statutory and recurrence explanations are noncontrolling.

**Thomas, concurring in part and dissenting in part, joined by Scalia throughout and Kennedy only in Part II.** He joins the Court's payment-based threshold discussion but would affirm both statutory dismissals. Part I first reads State or political subdivision as the covered governments and their organs, rather than every association whose conduct might count as constitutional state action. Sheffield's governmental-body holding does not erase that distinction; Congress used broader person/under-color-of-law language elsewhere. The regulation cannot extend the statute, and a litigant's legal concession about it cannot determine the meaning of the presented coverage question.

Alternatively, he finds Virginia's recognition, ballot benefits and limited requirements insufficient to establish the governmental delegation or effective substitution for an election that he regards as necessary. Smith and Terry retain their constitutional force, but do not make this private nomination a state election on these facts. He independently reads §14(c)(1)'s primary, special and general elections as excluding conventions: party-office and effective-vote language does not erase that list, and §2's later amendment did not amend these provisions. His actual Holder ballot-access position remains noncontrolling and is not substituted for the Court's §2 law.

His association/avoidance ground also incorporates Scalia's overbreadth, uncertainty, prior-restraint and avoidance objections. Party funding, membership and organization are substantial choices; denial of preclearance could require admission of those unwilling or unable to pay. The asserted financing justification remains advocacy. These grounds support his statutory construction, not a facial decree invalidating §5 or a final disposition of the separate constitutional counts. An appropriate challenge to a State's own discriminatory electoral practice remains distinct. No unverified Williams rationale supplies an independent holding.

Part II denies a private §10 action. In his view, the provision's declaration and express direction to the Attorney General lack the private statutory command found in Allen's §5 setting. General private-enforcement references in §§3, 12 and 14 and the 1975 amendment do not establish this additional action. Congressional intent, not usefulness, controls. Actual Central Bank preserves its confined received securities action; his contrary position there supplies no contrary Court holding. He would affirm without deciding whether the charge is an unlawful poll tax, awarding money or denying all constitutional voting remedies.

**Scalia, concurring in part and dissenting in part, joined throughout by Thomas.** He joins Part I of the Court opinion and Thomas's entire separate opinion. His additional explanation treats candidate selection as central expressive association. Preclearance requires prior federal permission even for lawful changes, imposes the burden of establishing nondiscriminatory purpose and effect, and subjects convention timing and choices to governmental control. That is the concrete prior-restraint concern; it cannot be dismissed as mere regulation of customer identity under Hurley.

He also objects to overbreadth and chilling uncertainty. Even if this isolated fee could constitutionally require submission, the interpretation's reach across protected party activity must be addressed. Leaving the covered class indefinite can chill current conduct; reserving every difficult application for later supplies neither the limiting construction nor the overbreadth treatment he considers necessary. The substantial constitutional doubt favors the statute's express reference to States and political subdivisions rather than imposing this restraint on parties.

Congress could address some discriminatory practices through other provisions without extending §5 to every party procedure. References to party office elsewhere do not prove the distinct preclearance duty. Those statutory and avoidance grounds, together with Thomas's §10 analysis, support affirmance. The opinion declares neither facial invalidity of the Act or regulation nor immunity from constitutional law, and decides no fee merits or refund.

**Kennedy, concurring in part and dissenting in part.** He joins Part I of the Court opinion and only Part II of Thomas's separate opinion. His independent §5 ground distinguishes a statutory covered government from every person whose conduct may be attributed to the State under constitutional doctrine. Congress named governments here while using broader private-person language elsewhere; ordinary ballot recognition and preserved party autonomy do not impose the asserted direct submission duty on the Party.

A State's own change making party practices legally operative or facilitating discriminatory nomination can remain subject to §5 as a state practice. That governmental-responsibility inquiry differs from requiring the Party to submit every procedure because its nominee receives ballot benefits. He does not decide whether these appellants would prevail under constitutional state-action principles, the full reach of Congress's Reconstruction Amendment powers or Thomas's separate convention-definition theory. Smith and Terry remain available for the constitutional claims in their existing posture.

He also identifies serious costs in placing party procedure under prior control of a politically accountable federal officer, without alleging misconduct. That concern would support avoidance if ambiguity existed; his statutory entity reading is an independent ground. His §10 objection is the specific congressional-intent analysis in Thomas's Part II, consistent with distinguishing development within an established action from creation of a new one. He would affirm both statutory dismissals without deciding fee legality or monetary relief.

Authority and exact joins: [Public decision](../records/Morse_v_Republican_Party_of_Virginia_merits_1996-03-27.md).

### Rutledge v. United States, No. 94-8769; 517 U.S. 292 — March 27, 1996

Chief Justice Stone-Zsela concurs in part and dissents in part. He begins with Blockburger's element comparison and the offenses as charged and tried. Here the CCE verdict necessarily incorporated the same agreement and concerted conduct supporting conspiracy, so every element of the §846 count was necessarily established. His conclusion is confined to that elements-and-trial structure; it does not bar convictions for distinct conspiracies or offenses requiring an element not necessarily included in the CCE count.

Ball makes the second judgment consequential even though imprisonment runs concurrently. The separate assessment, stigma and other collateral effects prevent treating the included conviction as an empty entry. On that basis, the Double Jeopardy Clause requires removal of the included judgment. His partial joins adopt the corresponding case-specific application, second-conviction consequences and assessment correction; they do not adopt the Court's broader statutory construction, fuller congressional-intent analysis, preservation ruling or future appellate-entry proposition.

His remedial disagreement is concrete. Because conspiracy is the included offense established by this CCE verdict, he would direct vacatur of Count 2 and its special assessment and leave the CCE conviction and sentence undisturbed. He therefore agrees that the dual-conviction ruling must be reversed but dissents from allowing the District Court to vacate CCE instead. No other Justice joins his separate writing.

Authority and exact joins: [Public decision](../records/Rutledge_v_United_States_merits_1996-03-27.md).

### Seminole Tribe of Florida v. Florida, No. 94-12; 517 U.S. 44 — March 27, 1996

**Stone-Zsela, concurring in part and dissenting in part.** He joins the officer holding and statutory limits and supports removal of Florida's dismissal direction, but would affirmatively sustain Congress's clearly enacted prospective direct-State action. Indian Commerce authority, the ongoing federal duty and unmistakable authorization support that route. Prospective compliance costs do not become accrued treasury compensation merely because payment is needed. Congress's express enforcement channel and the Tribe's continuing-duty claim warrant retaining a forum. Young independently reaches the connected officer, with the same statutory restraints. Neither route permits a preferred compact, bypassed mediation, enlarged duty or disguised retrospective damages; lawful relief should avoid double or inconsistent commands.

He expressly refuses to treat officer availability as sufficient reason to stop short of sustaining the State action. He retains Union Gas's actual damages judgment without adopting every broader abrogation rationale. He reserves materially new compensatory, punitive or restitutionary liability, compulsory state-court actions and different statutory schemes, while recognizing that already-decided Union Gas questions remain settled within its scope. He supplies no new waiver or Reconstruction ground.

**Stevens, concurring in part and dissenting in part.** He joins Parts II–III and would sustain both routes. Outside the Eleventh Amendment's actual textual restriction, Hans immunity is judicial doctrine subject to displacement by valid congressional legislation. IGRA supplies the affirmative direction absent from Hans; Congress cannot amend the Constitution or exceed Article III. His rationale is not confined to prospective Indian Commerce litigation and does not require overruling Hans's actual result. He retains Union Gas's constitutional conclusion and leaves the textual issue concerning out-of-state or foreign-citizen plaintiffs open; the Tribe is not treated as such a plaintiff. His own remedial-intent analysis supports the constrained officer action, and he accepts lawful officer-only resolution as a narrower sufficient alternative without abandoning his affirmative State position.

He nevertheless retains serious doubt whether this intermediate judicial step, particularly if separate executive relief could make it dispensable, is fully judicial under Article III. That is a reservation, not a vote to dismiss independently. Wisconsin's partial-redress holding does not settle this different judicial-function issue. He does not formally join Souter's entire separate theory.

**Souter, joined by Ginsburg and Breyer, respecting the State claim in Part IV.** They prefer the established officer route and vacatur of Florida's immunity-dismissal direction without deciding abrogation. Intricate remedies and State wording alone do not clearly exclude received prospective equity; Congress may limit statutory enforcement, but they find no sufficient indication of exclusion here. This is distinct from inventing a personal damages action. They would address whether State adjudication is necessary in light of lawful officer relief while preserving lawful jurisdiction before State merits adjudication or a proper nonmerits resolution. The Tribe might forgo its State claim or adequate officer relief might support denying duplicative relief, but neither fact is found. They prescribe no automatic abandonment, mootness, dismissal or indefinite stay. Their additional sequence is not the Court's mandate.

If Young were rejected and Florida's still-live immunity claim adjudicated, they would recognize the direct-State clear statement and uphold congressional displacement of Hans immunity under valid Article I power. They regard that nontextual immunity as federal common law, retained by stare decisis absent deliberate legislative displacement, rather than constitutional immunity Congress can never alter. Constitutional text, limited prior holdings and legislative control of common law independently support that account; it is not a wholesale adoption of Brennan's Union Gas reasoning. Their view is not confined to prospective relief or commerce, but decides no damages or unrelated statute. Because Young succeeds here, these constitutional views remain conditional alternatives, not actual joins in a State-amenability holding.

**O'Connor, joined by Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas, concurring in part and dissenting in part.** They join the judicial-character ruling and find unmistakable direct-State intent, but would affirm both dismissals. Their constitutional rule is broad: original Article I powers cannot overcome the constitutional immunity limiting federal judicial power over a nonconsenting State. Prospective relief does not cure the defect; neither Indian/interstate commerce nor proprietary/governmental distinctions justifies retaining Union Gas. They would expressly overrule its constitutional conclusion while leaving its statutory construction and Fitzpatrick's later Fourteenth Amendment authority intact.

They acknowledge Union Gas's five-vote constitutional conclusion rather than declaring it never precedent. In their view its conflict with the constitutional immunity structure, fractured rationale and deficient integration with prior immunity decisions supply the special justification for correction. They reject the opposing distinction between a common-law default and congressional displacement, without inventing zero reliance or proof that clear-statement rules are empirically unworkable. Their premise does not adjudicate every other statute or remedy, grant immunity to every public entity, foreclose United States enforcement or eliminate ordinary Young relief.

Independently, they read IGRA as selecting the State-party action, reciprocal State/Tribe order and limited subsequent progression. An ordinary officer injunction risks judicial coercion Congress withheld, but their objection is not limited to unlimited contempt: even an officer action copying the deadlines changes Congress's selected defendant and enforcement form. The sovereign-compacting arrangement reinforces that inference. They recognize that Congress can authorize constrained officer remedies; they conclude it did not do so here. They establish no universal detailed-scheme bar, no categorical affirmative-duty exception to Young, and no power to rewrite the Act merely because enforcement otherwise has a gap.

Authority and exact joins: [Public decision](../records/Seminole_Tribe_of_Florida_v_Florida_merits_1996-03-27.md).

Chief Justice Stone-Zsela concurs while joining the Court's opinion. Financial leave provides an opportunity for consideration, not endorsement of a petition or entitlement to certiorari. Each of these declarations and papers satisfies the conditions for that opportunity; neither one adequate affidavit nor one defective allegation can resolve the other motions.

### Bowersox v. Williams, application No. A-828; 517 U.S. 345 — April 9, 1996

**Chief Justice Alex-Lamar Stone-Zsela, concurring in part and dissenting in part.** I join Part I's reservation of final disposition and immediate record examination. Execution before the Court can identify the lower court's substantial grounds would make review irretrievable. Lack of an explanation calls for one; it does not establish that a successive habeas claim is substantial.

I would direct the lower court to supply its stay order, reasons, identified claims and relevant successive-petition findings within two hours after service of the order, with concise party responses within two further hours. I would also administratively stay execution until the full Court resolves the dissolution application or twelve hours after service, whichever occurs first, unless the Court expressly extends protection. The Court must review the matter before expiration, and the Clerk must confirm actual notice to the executing authorities. Those are my proposed terms, not additional relief entered by the Court.

The short administrative interval would preserve the ability to decide the actual application. It would neither dissolve nor adjudge valid the Eighth Circuit stay. Delo v. Blair's equal division supplies no controlling rationale; McFarland's preparation rule and Schlup's gateway retain their own predicates. I select no final grant or denial. The Court's different implementation and decision to issue no additional execution stay are not my proposed disposition.

**Justice John Paul Stevens.** I support the bounded reservation and immediate examination specified in the order and adopt Kennedy's Parts I–III. The actual basis of the challenged stay must be examined before this application is decided. This procedural action decides neither the stay's ultimate propriety nor any habeas claim.

**Justice Sandra Day O'Connor.** I support the bounded reservation and immediate examination specified in the order and adopt Kennedy's Parts I–III. The successive-petition standard remains governing; the certificate and the unexplained order do not themselves answer it. No new execution stay is granted.

**Justice Antonin Scalia.** I support the bounded reservation and immediate examination specified in the order and adopt Kennedy's Parts I–III. The State is entitled to prompt consideration of its application on the actual grounds. The reservation confers no entitlement to further delay.

**Justice Anthony M. Kennedy.** I support the bounded reservation and immediate examination specified in the order for the reasons in Parts I–III. Prompt consideration on the relevant papers protects the lawful interests of both parties. Any further judicial action must rest on its own basis.

**Justice David H. Souter.** I support the bounded reservation and immediate examination specified in the order and adopt Kennedy's Parts I–III. This permits examination of the actual appellate basis without treating the certificate or the petition's number as dispositive.

**Justice Clarence Thomas.** I support the bounded reservation and immediate examination specified in the order and adopt Kennedy's Parts I–III. The actual claims and prior dispositions are necessary to apply the successive-petition rules. This order creates no additional habeas entitlement.

**Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg.** I support the bounded reservation and immediate examination specified in the order and adopt Kennedy's Parts I–III. The need for further process or protection must be established on the actual papers. Neither is found by this procedural action.

**Justice Stephen G. Breyer.** I support the bounded reservation and immediate examination specified in the order and adopt Kennedy's Parts I–III. The application returns promptly for decision; no unknown claim, procedural exception or stay duration is resolved now.

Authority and exact joins: [Public decision](../records/Bowersox_v_Williams_interim_application_order_1996-04-09.md).

### Bowersox v. Williams — final application order — April 9, 1996

**Justice Sandra Day O'Connor, signed final Circuit Justice explanation and Opinion of the Court.** I grant the application for the reasons in Parts I–V. The identified cause, repeated-instruction, distinct second-degree and amendment grounds do not satisfy the substantial-grounds standard. The available noncapital options answer the Beck issue; the assumed state-rule inconsistency does not add the federal deprivation shown in Hicks. My explanation removes the challenged stay without deciding entitlement to the writ or directing execution.

**Justice Antonin Scalia.** I vote to grant the application and vacate the March 8 stay. I adopt O'Connor's Parts I–V, including their separate grounds and limits.

**Justice Anthony M. Kennedy.** I vote to grant the application and vacate the March 8 stay. I adopt O'Connor's Parts I–V, including their separate grounds and limits.

**Justice David H. Souter.** I vote to grant the application and vacate the March 8 stay. I adopt O'Connor's Parts I–V, including their separate grounds and limits.

**Justice Clarence Thomas.** I vote to grant the application and vacate the March 8 stay. I adopt O'Connor's Parts I–V, including their separate grounds and limits.

**Justice John Paul Stevens, dissenting.** I would deny the application. A State's creation of a particular jury opportunity is not made immaterial by a different lawful noncapital option. Schad controls the minimum Beck safeguard; the available second-degree claim raises the distinct Hicks question whether inconsistent withholding of the state-created option was arbitrary. The reported intent and kidnapping dispute gives that question potential consequence. It warrants appellate consideration without establishing a violation, a writ or an automatic successive-petition stay. I need not decide an independent equal-protection ground or the other claims.

**Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, dissenting.** I would deny the application. Genuine noncapital alternatives answer Beck but do not conclusively answer arbitrary deprivation of the separately available state-law opportunity under Hicks. On the assumed availability and inconsistent treatment, that due-process question is substantial enough for meaningful appellate examination. I find no proved violation or independent equal-protection ground and rely neither on the certificate alone nor on unknown papers. The existing stay would remain subject to lawful modification, without a new Supreme Court stay or guaranteed duration.

**Justice Stephen G. Breyer, dissenting.** I would deny the application. The available Hicks question could affect the conviction or sentence on the reported intent and kidnapping evidence. Absence of an all-or-nothing choice under Schad does not conclusively resolve the alleged arbitrary withholding of a further state-created jury opportunity. That concrete issue, rather than uncertainty or the certificate, supplies substantial grounds. Ultimate relief remains undecided; I require no new hearing, gateway or protection through every appellate step and need not decide the other claims.

**Chief Justice Alex-Lamar Stone-Zsela, dissenting.** I would deny the application. The available second-degree claim presents a substantial question whether Missouri arbitrarily withheld a state-created jury opportunity when it refused an available instruction differently from materially similar cases. The reported dispute about intent and the kidnapping gives that question potential consequence. Hicks protects against arbitrary deprivation of a state-created opportunity. Schad establishes that genuine noncapital verdict options satisfy Beck's minimum safeguard; it does not conclusively resolve this distinct due-process issue. Availability alone does not establish a mandatory instruction duty, and the assumed inconsistency does not prove a constitutional violation. The question is substantial enough for the existing appeal, although ultimate relief remains undecided. Denial would leave the appellate stay governed by its own terms and subject to lawful modification. I would issue no new Supreme Court stay, guarantee no particular duration, and adopt no independent ground on the other claims.

Authority and exact joins: [Public decision](../records/Bowersox_v_Williams_final_application_disposition_1996-04-09.md).

### Miller — published dissents, April 15

**Justice Scalia, dissenting, joined by Justice Thomas.** They would reverse the facial invalidation of the minor-notice condition and conform relief accordingly, leaving the unrelated rulings untouched. They retain their constitutional objection to Casey's heightened abortion framework and regard the actual one-parent notice duty, finite interval and emergency and abuse accommodations as reasonable means of protecting minors and parental responsibility. The abuse definition reaches threatened harm, and its confidentiality duty is a real statutory protection. In their view, the Federal Constitution does not require the additional maturity or best-interests mechanism the Court demands.

They recognize the Court's practical-obstruction evidence but reject the constitutional premise that places these supported notice burdens within the majority's heightened sequence. Approval of Pennsylvania's available bypass establishes its permissibility, not a general duty to enact one elsewhere. Their disagreement is with the governing constitutional rule and its justification burden; it does not authorize lower courts to disregard Casey or depend on an independent numerical facial bar. They do not decide every hypothetical emergency or wrongful-enforcement claim.

**Justice Kennedy, dissenting.** He would reverse this facial minor-notice invalidation and conform the decree to that result. He retains protected choice and the prohibition on effective control expressed in Casey, but rejects the general residual lesser-burden allocation that requires the State to answer the Court's independent-authorization alternative here. A parent's responsibility for a minor differs from a spouse's control over another adult. The actual law requires notice rather than consent and contains emergency, threatened-harm and confidentiality protections with more reach than a completed-assault-only description suggests.

The honor-student episode and the reporting and disclosure concerns are material. In his assessment, the supplied incidents and predictions do not establish that this entire notice structure is an effective veto or that all mature minors must be exempted. He would preserve relief for a separately established unprotected instance of practical prevention or denial of necessary care, with an identified application and effective remedy. That reservation does not lead him to join the facial injunction. He does not treat Salerno as displacing the Court's controlling method, accept all parental obstruction, or join Scalia's rejection of the underlying constitutional protection.

### Cooper — April 16

All participating Justices join the Court's three Parts. No separate opinion is filed. [Public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Cooper_v_Oklahoma_merits_1996-04-16.md). No new noncontrolling position is added.

### Markman — published separate writing, April 23, 1996

**Chief Justice Stone-Zsela, concurring in part and in the judgment.** He joins Parts I and III and agrees that the noninfringement judgment should stand. Patent claims define a public legal boundary requiring authoritative, reasonably uniform judicial construction. That legal function remains distinct from deciding what the accused product does, whether evidence is credible and whether the product falls within the construed claim. Bischoff's construction/factual-identity distinction supports preserving both responsibilities.

He does not join Part II's assignment of genuinely disputed historical technical facts or credibility to the judge simply because they arise within construction. A construction label cannot itself remove a jury function; his reservation extends to genuine historical or credibility disputes embedded in determining meaning, not merely to external product-operation disputes. Uniform patent administration supports judicial legal meaning but does not supply authority to relabel protected factual work.

That disagreement requires no different judgment here. Crediting the supported cash/invoice usage and technical testimony still leaves this instrument's article-related requirement intact. No witness must be disbelieved, and the established concession resolves infringement under the clothing-inclusive construction. He therefore joins the Court's actual interpretation and independently sufficient JMOL application without endorsing the broader embedded-dispute allocation. He proposes no new hearing, factual finding, infringement judgment or remand and adopts no universal subsidiary appellate-review rule.

Authority: [public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Markman_v_Westview_Instruments_Inc_merits_1996-04-23.md).

### Holly Farms — published separate writing, April 23, 1996

Justice O'Connor, joined by Scalia and Thomas, concurs in Parts I–III and dissents from Part IV and the resulting affirmance for catchers and forklift operators. Her opinion gives effect to both secondary-agriculture requirements: these workers perform on-farm preparation directly connected to the poultry raised on that farm. The on-farm route permits nonfarmer employees, and preparation can accompany farming even when a purchaser controls the schedule and also benefits. The conditional preparation-for-market provisions and the described poultry-cooping/loading interpretations support that application; they do not make every activity on a farm agricultural.

The separate opinion accepts that the Board actually relied on integration and that a separately organized business may fall outside agriculture. It finds the actual catching and loading here remain farm preparation, rather than slaughter, dressing or other processing conducted on the premises. Plant coordination does not negate that direct relationship, and the statute requires neither exclusive farming purpose nor employment by the grower. Bayside's by-farmer ruling does not resolve these on-farm acts. The direct statutory relation controls this application; deference within genuine ambiguity does not permit the Board to remove it. The opinion preserves driver coverage and does not reach the primary-harvesting merits.

The three would reverse inclusion of catchers and forklift operators, vacate enforcement of the bargaining order only to the extent dependent on the improperly constituted unit, and remand through the court of appeals for appropriate Board reconsideration of the lawful unit, the earlier authorization-card majority and the Gissel remedy. The 95–95 election establishes neither a current majority nor automatic termination of that inquiry. Workforce numbers cannot supply card counts. No particular replacement unit, new election, evidentiary hearing or new bargaining order would be directed. Unrelated findings involving covered workers and Tyson's separate successorship issue would remain undisturbed except for any actual remedial dependence on the reversed classification. These proposed consequences are the minority's remedy, not the Court's mandate.

Authority: [public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Holly_Farms_Corp_v_NLRB_merits_1996-04-23.md).

### Carlisle — published dissent, April 29

**Justice Stevens, dissenting, joined by Justice Kennedy.** They would reverse the no-authority ruling and remand for appellate consideration of the Government's disputed sufficiency ground. Their source of power is the court's retained pre-sentence judicial authority to prevent judgment on legally insufficient evidence, informed by the acquittal duty recognized in Rule 29(a). They do not treat that subdivision alone as an unrestricted postverdict motion remedy.

They accept that Rules 29(c) and 45(b) foreclose the defendant's late-motion entitlement, but do not read those provisions as withdrawing the judge's distinct authority while the case awaits sentence. Smith's completed-appellate setting makes its finality concern materially different. Manypenny's timely-motion holding does not itself decide this further question, but recognizes judicial correction within a continuing proceeding. Williams supplies an example of bounded supervision; it is not a license to disregard a controlling rule. On their reading, no rule withdraws the particular power asserted here.

The Court's strongest objection is that this construction allows the same relief the time limit restricts and substitutes sentencing for the specified deadline. The dissent answers that the source and function differ: a lost party motion does not compel entry of a judgment the judge concludes lacks legal evidentiary support. The position is confined to that pre-sentence responsibility, not a one-day, no-prejudice or general fairness exception, and it does not reopen completed criminal judgments indefinitely.

The dissent does not decide that the evidence was insufficient or that Carlisle was factually innocent. The Government contested the sufficiency ruling, and the Sixth Circuit did not resolve it. Acquittal therefore could not finally be restored without that review. The dissent orders neither a new trial nor release and does not rely on an unrestricted collateral remedy or automatic judicial-assurance exception.

Authority: [public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Carlisle_v_United_States_merits_1996-04-29.md).

### Sheets — published dissent, April 29

Justice Scalia, joined by Thomas, dissents. He accepts for purposes of review the supported intentional disclosure, causation and Gary's own intimate injury, but finds no established constitutional guarantee of the asserted kind. Whalen deliberately reserved unwarranted dissemination, and Nixon sustained protected governmental screening rather than recognizing this damages entitlement. Decisional-autonomy precedents do not themselves establish general control over information held by government. Paul's refusal to constitutionalize the arrest-record claim reinforces the need to identify the actual federal guarantee, without making every intimate disclosure identical to reputation harm.

The dissent therefore finds the majority's extension unsupported even though the conduct may violate a promise, state duties or ordinary privacy expectations. Scalia's Albright source objection and Thomas's distinct insistence on a demonstrated substantive guarantee support that conclusion; they do not establish a general rule that state tort remedies cure an otherwise recognized substantive violation. Hodge left this merits question open. The dissent does not infer prior publication from archive availability, deny the accepted intimate injury, make Kathy's authorship dispositive or require tangible economic loss.

The two would reverse the reviewed constitutional ruling, vacate the federal judgment dependent on this right and remand for disposition consistent with rejection of the §1983 theory. Consequential prevailing-party fee treatment would follow under governing law. They direct no new factual trial, state-tort adjudication, refund amount or independent fee rule, and make no new ruling on personal immunity or the reasonableness of the awards.

Authority: [public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Sheets_v_Salt_Lake_County_merits_1996-04-29.md).

### Armstrong — published positions, May 13

**Breyer, concurring in part and in the judgment.** He joins Parts II–III but rejects Part I's Rule 16 exclusion. Paragraph (a)(1)(C)'s three disjunctive categories perform different work; its defense-preparation category is not confined to the Government's evidence in chief. Information material to a genuine selective-prosecution defense can therefore fall within the Rule, subject to its independent exclusions and protections. Here the missing relevant comparison defeats materiality, so he agrees that the order and dependent dismissal fail. Kimberlin and Klinger preserve grounded circumstantial proof, but disproportionate access and a less intrusive proposed stage cannot supply an absent predicate. He does not resolve a necessary work-product exception, promise enforceable access to all state records or eliminate a distinct lawful source of discovery.

**Stone-Zsela, concurring in part and dissenting in part.** He joins Part II and would expressly vacate the unsupported-order dismissal, but would remand for a staged, limited inquiry under an attainable, evidence-based threshold. The selected 24-defendant sample does not identify comparably eligible non-Black offenders treated differently, supply the denominator or itself prove discriminatory purpose. Kimberlin forbids categorical direct-proof demands; it does not compel his proposed charging procedure or erase effect, purpose and relevant comparison.

His proposed remand would assess the comparison in its offense, eligibility, place and time context with available purpose evidence. These are reliability considerations, not a mandatory checklist or a demand for every listed form of proof. Reliable jurisdiction-specific data, concrete indications of comparably eligible offenders and a supported reason missing information lies with the prosecutor can justify narrow production. A specifically justified alternative evidentiary basis must be accepted where comparator names cannot reasonably be obtained. If the threshold is met, inquiry would begin with limited comparable data or interrogatories, appropriate redaction, privilege review and protective orders, expanding only if the response warrants it. The existing broad order would not return on this sample alone. Ordinary prosecution would resume unless lawful new proceedings justify another remedy. His proposal establishes neither automatic discovery, racial discrimination nor acquittal, and his directed staged remand is not the Court's mandate.

**Stevens, dissenting.** He would affirm the reviewed judgment. Respondents established neither the selective-prosecution defense nor a right to discovery under Rule 16 or inherent authority. That lack of entitlement does not, in his view, eliminate the district judge's bounded discretion to inquire into a disturbing evidentiary pattern. The defined all-Black sample, Reed's firsthand state/federal experience, the substantial federal/state penalty difference and the judge's consideration of the developed response justified inquiry appreciably short of merits proof. Relayed observations and firsthand experience should not be conflated, and the absence of a Government admissibility objection below does not establish a universal hearsay rule.

Wayte's constitutional limits, Williams's bounded judicial protection and the distinction between failed party entitlement and retained judicial function support his discretionary ground. Wade's screening requirement and the mismatch between general crack cases and these federal charges remain serious limits; they do not make every inquiry an abuse of discretion. He acknowledges that the order may have been broader than necessary, but does not replace his affirmance with a criteria-only remand or unconditional access to protected files. He supplies no representative denominator, merits discrimination finding or shifted ultimate burden, and would not give the Government a new unconditional opportunity to refuse, obtain review and then comply after losing.

Authority: [public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_United_States_v_Armstrong_merits_1996-05-13.md).

### 44 Liquormart — published positions, May 13

**Kennedy's noncontrolling Parts IV-A–C.** In IV-A, joined by Stevens, Souter and Ginsburg, he emphasizes the consumer's interest in accurate commercial information and the special care appropriate when the State suppresses the entire relevant category to influence lawful purchases. That view is distinct from a rule invalidating every such restriction categorically. In IV-B, joined by Stevens and Ginsburg, he would apply more rigorous review to complete truthful-speech suppression unrelated to protecting consumers from deception or comparable injury. It is not announced as universal strict scrutiny for commercial speech. These Justices also adopt the narrower independently sufficient applications in I and II; Stevens's informational objection is not reduced to insufficient evidence alone.

In IV-C, joined by Stevens, Thomas and Ginsburg, Kennedy rejects Posadas's highly deferential permission to choose informational suppression for paternalistic ends, the inference that power to prohibit a product necessarily includes power to suppress truthful promotion, and a freestanding lawful-vice exception. This does not repudiate every Posadas holding. Thomas's join in this treatment does not add a balancing vote, and Souter does not join it. None of these portions commands five votes.

**O'Connor, concurring in part and in the judgment, joined by Breyer.** They join II, III-A and V-A–B. Ordinary Central Hudson/Fox review suffices, with temperance substantial and advancement assumed. Economic prediction and expert concessions deserve genuine weight; they do not decide that the State necessarily fails the advancement prong. The permanent burden on all covered truthful price references nevertheless lacks proportional fit in light of concrete direct controls. Their prior support for supported prophylaxis and finite privacy restrictions does not validate this different burden. They require neither definitive empirical proof nor selection of the least restrictive policy. They distinguish LaRue's licensed-premises conduct and apply subsequent searching doctrine rather than join III-B or IV-C. No new tier, categorical anti-paternalism ground or interstate rule is necessary. Souter joins Part II's independent fit ground, but does not join this separate writing or withdraw his affirmative advancement holding.

**Scalia, concurring in part and in the judgment.** He joins III-A–B and V-A–B. Existing commercial-speech jurisprudence supports invalidation, but he does not expressly join either the advancement or fit analysis and declines to develop or reinforce the doctrine through a new test here. His doubts about Central Hudson and distaste for governmental paternalism do not themselves supply a replacement constitutional rule. The available historical-practice account is inadequate for that change in this case. He nevertheless joins the broader Twenty-first Amendment treatment and preservation of LaRue's conduct holding, but not the broader Posadas passage. His agreement with the result is not another vote for either sufficient balancing ground.

**Thomas, concurring in part and in the judgment.** He joins III-A–B, IV-C and V-A–B, and independently regards the asserted interest in keeping lawful purchasers ignorant in order to manipulate their choices as per se illegitimate. Successful informational suppression would not cure that defect. He does not join Central Hudson balancing, an assumption legitimizing that informational objective, a failure-of-proof rationale or the Fox holding. His rule does not decide whether balancing remains appropriate for materially different interests. It reaches Peoples' presented lawful-sale information as well as 44 Liquormart's speech, while leaving unresolved its relationship to Edge when the forum State has prohibited or regulated the underlying domestic transaction. His broader Posadas and Twenty-first Amendment positions do not overrule Edge by implication. His agreement with the implementing remand rests on his categorical ground and does not adopt the Court's balancing analyses.

**Stone-Zsela, concurring in the constitutional judgment and specified Court portions, and dissenting in part as to remedy.** He joins I, II, III-A and V-A. Ordinary Central Hudson review resolves the case: temperance is substantial, the actual proof does not demonstrate material alleviation, and direct controls reveal inadequate fit. He endorses neither a heightened tier nor a categorical anti-paternalism rule. He does not join the broader LaRue or Posadas treatment. He would expressly enjoin enforcement of the challenged ban against truthful, nonmisleading retail-price advertising, rather than stop at the declaration-preserving remand, and therefore does not join V-B. His injunction would preserve otherwise lawful direct regulation of alcohol sales, prices, taxes, hours and unlawful promotions. False, misleading and transaction-integral advertising remain subject to applicable regulation; his position creates no general immunity for alcohol marketing.

Authority: [public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_44_Liquormart_Inc_v_Rhode_Island_merits_1996-05-13.md).

### Noland — published positions, May 13

All nine Justices join the Court's opinion. No separate opinion is filed.

Authority: [public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_United_States_v_Noland_merits_1996-05-13.md).

### Brown Group — published positions, May 13

All participating Justices join the Court's two Parts. No separate opinion is filed.

Authority: [public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_United_Food_and_Commercial_Workers_Union_Local_751_v_Brown_Group_Inc_merits_1996-05-13.md).

### Romer — published noncontrolling positions, May 20

**Scalia, dissenting, joined by Thomas.** The two Justices would reverse the reviewed equal-protection judgment and remove that foundation for the injunction, with remand bounded by any independently preserved unresolved claims. They reject an extension of Hunter and Seattle into a fundamental entitlement of every group to pursue legislation at every governmental level, and they would sustain the amendment under ordinary rationality.

They accept its full restriction on state as well as local institutions, including public and nonintimate settings. In their view, regulatory restraint, religious and associational choice, finite enforcement resources and statewide uniformity rationally support withholding the disputed antidiscrimination protection. Reasonable predictions and imperfect coverage suffice; narrower exemptions are not constitutionally mandatory. The breadth implements the substantive policy rather than defeating its connection to those purposes. Constitutional reservation does not immunize the policy from federal review, but neither makes an otherwise rational policy unconstitutional.

Bowers is a sufficient additional premise in their reasoning: constitutional power to criminalize the specified conduct supports the lesser choice of withholding the disputed protection. Conduct-based moral judgment is distinct from hatred of persons, and orientation may serve as a proxy in this noncriminal policy. They do not claim Bowers literally adjudicated Amendment 2 or that every moral dislike is legitimate. Moreno and Cleburne continue to forbid bare harm; the dissent finds legitimate policy grounds here. Heller's controlling proof holding is distinguished as addressing an inadequately justified confinement risk, not displaced by its opposing opinion.

Their conditional facial argument also respects the state construction. If orientation, conduct, practices and relationships identify the same class, the Bowers inference, on their view, reaches the common operation. If a distinct orientation-only application is instead posited, constitutionally permissible conduct applications would defeat wholesale invalidation under their Salerno argument. That contention depends on their rejection of the Court's defect throughout the actual class-wide operation; it does not independently answer that defect. They order no severance, find no conduct by every class member and rely on no unverified admission by a respondent.

Scalia's commercial-speech position supplies no general prohibition of conduct-based moral legislation. Thomas's rejection of suppressing independently protected truthful speech, and his separate rule against keeping lawful purchasers ignorant to manipulate their choices, remain confined to that speech setting; he does not extend them into a universal bar on the different Bowers inference. Neither Justice treats actual religious conflicts as automatic exemptions for every ordinance. Their proposed remand would not adjudicate surviving First Amendment claims, invent a new hearing or authorize enforcement despite any independent lawful restraint. Their grounds and disposition are noncontrolling.

Authority: [public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Romer_v_Evans_merits_1996-05-20.md).

### BMW — published noncontrolling positions, May 20

**Breyer, concurring, joined by O'Connor and Souter.** All three join the Court's opinion in full and supply an additional explanation. A procedurally proper award ordinarily deserves a strong presumption of validity. Here both the standards' failure significantly to constrain discretion as interpreted and applied and the gross disproportion to legitimate punitive objectives overcome that presumption. The existence of hearings, state criteria and actual appellate correction is acknowledged.

Clear-and-convincing proof of punitive entitlement does not distinguish every permissible amount. Harm, culpability and profit criteria must constrain the actual sum; wealth and litigation incentives do not supply a missing limit, and inapplicable mitigation factors do not do so. A supported economic theory can provide meaningful discipline, but a hypothetical model cannot replace the grounds and evidence before the state court. Historical comparisons illustrate the concern without creating a damages formula. The concurrence neither invalidates Alabama's system on its face nor requires written arithmetic, a compulsory economic model or an automatic new trial. Its conjunctive rationale is supported by three Justices, not an additional Court holding.

**Scalia, dissenting, joined by Thomas.** They would affirm. Their substantive/process distinction preserves traditional adjudication and meaningful judicial review enforcing state-law limits while rejecting an independent federal constitutional entitlement to a different punitive sum. They regard the guideposts as lacking a sufficient constitutional source and workable measure for federal supervision of amounts. Disagreement with a number does not prove the absence of a safeguard.

Alabama held a postverdict hearing, applied its review criteria, expressly removed the foreign multiplier and reduced the judgment. Assuming the identified error required correction, the correction occurred; they need not adopt the Court's territorial rule. Their position approves neither the original $4 million nor every possible remittitur. Both retain Oberg's amount-review protection; Thomas's agreement rests on his own TXO and Oberg positions, without adopting a separate opinion he did not join.

**Ginsburg, dissenting.** She would affirm from institutional restraint, federalism and respect for actual state correction. Alabama's courts addressed deliberate recurring fraud, considered their substantive criteria and comparison awards, and replaced the jury's national measure with a reduced judgment. The difficulty of supplying a workable federal scale counsels against displacing that state judgment here. Her concern is not answered simply by identifying a high ratio.

She does not join Scalia's categorical rejection of every substantive due-process protection or affirm by applying the Court's new guideposts. Her earlier reservation of a properly presented gross-excessiveness challenge remains meaningful. The present federal challenge does not justify additional intervention in light of the safeguards and correction actually supplied. State reform may address punitive practice, but proposed reforms are not treated as operative law, and a later disclosure amendment does not erase this adjudicated wrong. Her conclusion rests on the established review and correction.

**Stone-Zsela, concurring in Part II and otherwise dissenting.** He would affirm the remitted $2 million punitive judgment. His answer to the first question is yes: Alabama supplied a constitutionally sufficient remedy for the identified use of foreign transactions through meaningful review and its established, accepted remittitur procedure. His answer to the second is no: constitutionally adequate adjudication and meaningful review do not leave an additional federal substantive power to invalidate an amount merely because its magnitude or ratio appears excessive.

BMW's corporate form does not remove its property and procedural protections, but those protections do not themselves establish a substantive entitlement to the sum a federal judge prefers. Each claimed constitutional consequence requires its own source. TXO established no controlling ratio or general substantive formula; Oberg requires meaningful examination and lawful correction of the amount without supplying a maximum, mandatory remittitur or federal recalculation formula. That amount-review function cannot be reduced to checking punitive entitlement alone.

He agrees that Alabama cannot punish beyond its lawful authority and that relevant foreign evidence differs from foreign conduct made an independent object of punishment. Knowledge, intent, deliberateness, notice or a common policy may make such evidence relevant. Alabama expressly corrected its identified error; another potentially lawful remedy does not automatically become constitutionally necessary.

Compensation measures loss, while punitive damages serve punishment and deterrence. A large ratio alone cannot determine whether the latter rests on a lawful basis; nor does a large compensatory award justify any punishment. Reprehensibility, ratios and comparable sanctions may inform state-law or otherwise established review without becoming the Court's new constitutional elements. Courts retain meaningful amount review and correction of unlawful punitive availability, instructions, proof, considerations, procedural unfairness and statutory violations. Those examples are not an exhaustive checklist.

His conclusion neither makes punitive damages unreviewable nor authorizes punishment outside Alabama's lawful authority. It preserves traditional remittitur, restores no part of the original $4 million, and reserves whether every form of judicial alteration is permissible. He joins Part II's narrow territorial and evidentiary propositions, but not the Court's independent substantive framework, application or remand.

Authority: [public decision](../entering-law/PUBLIC_BMW_of_North_America_Inc_v_Gore_merits_1996-05-20.md).

### Henderson — published noncontrolling positions, May 20

[Public source](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Henderson_v_United_States_merits_1996-05-20.md).

Justice Thomas, joined by Justice O'Connor, would affirm. Congress may make a procedural requirement a condition of sovereign consent, and the dissent reads §742's particular service command separately from §743's general private-party practice instruction as doing so here. Sherwood, Block and Nordic Village require respect for the actual scope of consent; this is not a contention that every sentence in a waiver statute is jurisdictional. Meyer's broad agency clause and Carlisle's criminal procedural mechanism do not determine the SAA's differently structured waiver.

A judicial rule cannot enlarge that consent under §2072(b) and Rule 82. Congress itself enacted former Rule 4(j) and had power to change the waiver, but its general dismissal timetable does not sufficiently establish repeal of the retained special condition. Prompt service can satisfy both, and general authorized enlargement need not displace the special statute. The 1993 transition supplies no independent substantive enlargement.

Service on the United States Attorney after 148 days fails the surviving requirement even under a reasonable-dispatch reading and assuming good cause. The Rule 4 extension does not extend that separate condition. No universal number of days, adverse diligence finding or conclusion about day-47 Attorney General receipt is required. Pioneer and the American Pipe/McCormick analogy do not establish general authority to extend this consent condition. The dissent neither creates a new Rule 4 defect nor decides injury merits, separate due process or a right to timely refiling. The unestablished Rule 12 waiver route does not supply an alternative reversal of the jurisdictional condition. These propositions are noncontrolling.

### Casarotto — published noncontrolling positions, May 20

[Public source](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Doctors_Associates_Inc_v_Casarotto_merits_1996-05-20.md).

Justice Thomas joins Part I and dissents from the merits judgment. He reads the FAA's structure and its federal-court judicial directions as failing to create §2's substantive command to state tribunals. He would overrule Southland to that extent and affirm the Montana judgment on federal nonapplication, maintaining the ground stated in his Allied-Bruce dissent. Statutory stare decisis and reliance do not, in his view, cure that original construction error.

His participation in federal arbitration cases concerning assent or other statutes does not adopt Southland's state-court rule. The dissent does not conditionally uphold the notice law under a state-applicable §2, find a successful general contract defense, decide commerce coverage, announce an independently sufficient §§3–4 specific-performance rule or restrict Congress's constitutional power to enact a different command. It supplies no liability, damages or party-wide arbitration judgment. These proposed changes are noncontrolling.

### Pinder — published noncontrolling positions, May 21

[bounded public source](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Pinder_v_Johnson_merits_1996-05-21.md).

Justice Ginsburg, joined by Justices Stevens, Souter and Breyer, joins Parts I–II but would vacate the reviewed immunity disposition and remand. Injured-party custody is not indispensable where an official's own sufficiently culpable conduct actually removes otherwise available protection and thereby exposes the victims to a known immediate mortal danger. The dissent concludes now that the qualifying form of this alleged deprivation was sufficiently identified by pre-March 10, 1989 law to defeat immunity disposing of the entire theory at this stage.

Bowers's active-tortfeasor distinction, Archie's private-aid reasoning and Jensen's distinct danger discussion, read with DeShaney's no-increased-vulnerability limit, supply that particular principle. Their adverse outcomes and culpability restrictions remain material. Purposefully giving reassurance alone is insufficient; culpability must attach to the deprivation, and actual causal displacement must be shown. The dissent does not restore a knowledge-and-promise special relationship or infer notice from the deaths' severity. It disagrees with the en banc application to this account, not with an invented universal custody rule.

The favorable pleading possibility includes intentional or conscience-shocking deprivation without establishing that mental state. The dissent selects no minimum standard for every lesser account, finds no knowing falsity or favoritism, and does not assume greater charges would have prevented release. A later factual finding cannot create historical legal notice. Materially different or less culpable conduct retains its own constitutional and immunity analysis.

The requested remand would proceed through the Court of Appeals under ordinary preservation, pleading and proof rules, addressing culpability, actual causal predicates and genuinely available defenses only as needed. It would not unconditionally restore the entire district order or vacated panel opinion, mandate discovery, a hearing or trial, award damages, or adjudicate excluded counts. This bounded merits-and-notice position is noncontrolling.

### Ornelas — published positions, May 28

[bounded public source](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Ornelas_v_United_States_merits_1996-05-28.md).

Justice Scalia joins Part I but would affirm the reviewed allocation. Courts should independently correct legal definitions and legal-rule errors while deferring to the district court's concrete reasonable-suspicion and probable-cause applications under the circuit's clear-error formulation. Practical probabilities depend heavily on interacting circumstances and trial experience; many applications offer little reusable guidance. Pierce and Cooter & Gell demonstrate why that institutional comparison can favor ultimate deference even when a legal standard is applied.

Thompson's custody question and Salve Regina's state-law exposition do not require the same allocation for every mixed issue. Gates's practical observations remain relevant even though its warrant-issuance test does not directly govern this appeal. Magistrate referral does not eliminate the district judge's institutional responsibility or power to supplement the record.

Scalia regards the majority's combination of independent ultimate review and deference to contextual inferences as unstable: its factual and evaluative parts are often difficult to separate. He would preserve correction of legal errors and clear factual mistakes without independently repeating each final probability estimate. Deference would run to the district court, not a presumption that officers were correct. His response to the majority's warrant-incentive rationale also invokes Leon's distinct treatment of searches under warrants; it supplies no alternative good-faith holding on this search.

His proposed ultimate deference is noncontrolling. He does not decide suppression in the first instance, reopen inevitable discovery, resolve database disclosure or supply an immunity-style reasonable-error defense.

### Quackenbush — published positions, June 3

[bounded public source](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Quackenbush_v_Allstate_Insurance_Co_merits_1996-06-03.md).

**Justice Kennedy, concurring.** He joins the Court's opinion in full but would not rule out a future extension permitting dismissal of a damages action where a serious affront to federalism could be avoided in no other way. Comity and federalism have significance beyond the historic discretion to withhold equitable relief, and California has a substantial interest in administering insurance insolvencies. A stay retaining federal jurisdiction is the preferred means of accommodating that interest. The present case supplies no occasion to decide whether extraordinary circumstances could permit dismissal. He recognizes no current exception and does not find either a stay or exceptional dismissal warranted on this record.

**Justice Scalia, concurring.** He also joins the Court's opinion in full, understanding its restriction to foreclose Kennedy's suggested discretionary surrender of lawfully imposed nondiscretionary jurisdiction. Congress's lawful decision to confer that jurisdiction cannot itself constitute the federalism affront authorizing a court to refuse it. There is consequently no need to determine whether this record otherwise presents extraordinary circumstances. His response does not reject every retained-jurisdiction stay or disturb independently governed state-tax comity and forum-non-conveniens doctrines. No other Justice joins either concurrence.

### Smiley — published positions, June 3

[bounded public source](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Smiley_v_Citibank_South_Dakota_NA_merits_1996-06-03.md).

### Loving — published positions, June 3

[bounded public source](../entering-law/PUBLIC_Loving_v_United_States_merits_1996-06-03.md).

**Stevens, joined by Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer, concurring.** They join the Court's authority analysis while preserving the substantial question whether capital military prosecutions constitutionally require a connection to military service. *Solorio* addressed noncapital jurisdiction and does not itself resolve that extension. The actual military connections suffice for this case: Fay was an active-duty soldier killed on Fort Hood, and Sharbino was a retired Army sergeant. Their concurrence neither dismisses for want of jurisdiction nor adopts a new eligibility condition. Agreement with this disposition does not decide every military capital offense.

**Scalia, joined by O'Connor, concurring.** Congress may assign implementation responsibilities ancillary to the President's genuine executive and Commander-in-Chief functions; it may not lawfully transfer legislative power itself. An assignment can cross that constitutional boundary when its extent and absence of constraints amount to such a transfer. Congress's actual offense, penalty and limiting provisions keep this assignment within execution of enacted military law. Scalia's distinction in *Mistretta* between ancillary rulemaking and lawmaking divorced from an existing executive or judicial function explains his agreement. The concurrence also rejects English Parliament–Crown arrangements as a basis for allocating powers under this Constitution; historical jurisdiction inquiries such as *Solorio* concern a different question. That objection does not withhold a join from any portion of the Court's present opinion, which contains no English-history ground. It supplies no independent Article II authority to disregard Congress.

**Thomas, concurring in the judgment.** He sustains this enacted military scheme on the distinct constitutional responsibilities of Congress and the President concerning the armed forces. He assumes, without deciding, that additional aggravators are constitutionally necessary, and does not adopt the Court's use of nonmilitary delegation doctrine or a general capital-delegation framework. If the added protection were constitutionally unnecessary, that premise would remove the corresponding complaint; he does not hold that the factors are unnecessary. His military-specific deference operates within Congress's actual offense and punishment choices, consistently with constitutional and statutory scrutiny in *Weiss* and *Ryder*, and supplies no power to ignore their requirements. He reserves any view of congressional authority to alter the separation of powers outside this setting and rejects speculative English-history inferences. His separate sufficient ground supports the judgment alone.

#### Brown v. Pro Football, Inc.; No. 95-388. — 1996-06-20

Authority: [Brown v. Pro Football, Inc.; No. 95-388.](../records/Brown_v_Pro_Football_Inc_merits_1996-06-20.md).

##### Opinion Topology

Justice Breyer delivers the opinion of the Court, joined in full by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg. Justice Stevens dissents alone. The Court opinion's complete rule, explanation and remedy command eight votes.

##### Separate Writings

**Justice Stevens, dissenting.** Stevens distinguishes the protection of collective employee demands and consensual group negotiation from immunity for an employer-only agreement imposing a wage the union never accepted. Jewel Tea's negotiated working condition does not establish that the employer restraint here receives the same protection. Connell shows why lawfulness under labor law cannot alone eliminate an otherwise independent antitrust constraint. Stevens accepts that impasse need not end the bargaining relationship under Bonanno; continued bargaining duties nevertheless do not establish an affirmative license to suppress wage competition through concerted enforcement of the rejected wage. His position preserves lawful multiemployer negotiation and permits ordinary antitrust defenses to be considered. He would reverse the exemption ground and remand for the unresolved appellate issues, without automatically restoring the entire monetary and injunctive judgment.


#### Lane v. Peña, No. 95-365; October Term 1995. — 1996-06-20

Authority: [Lane v. Peña, No. 95-365; October Term 1995.](../records/Lane_v_Pena_merits_1996-06-20.md).

##### Opinion Topology

Justice Souter delivered the Opinion of the Court, joined in full by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas and Ginsburg. Justice Stevens dissented, joined in full by Justice Breyer.

##### Separate Writings

Justice Stevens dissents, joined by Justice Breyer. In their view, Congress's express extension of §504 to federal programs carries the remedial setting in which that prohibition already operated. Section 505's differentiated enforcement channels codify particular means of enforcement without withdrawing ordinary damages for the newly express federal obligation; the 1986 recognition of legal and equitable remedies reinforces that reading. They accept that consent must come from enacted law and that Franklin alone cannot waive immunity, but find the combined provisions sufficient and distinguish Nordic Village's ambiguous bankruptcy formulation. Treating §505's assistance language as a restriction on the separate federal-program obligation gives the remedial scheme an unwarranted gap. They would reverse the categorical damages bar and remand for litigation of entitlement, amount and any remaining lawful defense. They would neither award damages automatically nor reopen the injunction.


#### United States v. Reorganized CF&I Fabricators of Utah, Inc., No. 95-325; October Term 1995. — 1996-06-20

Authority: [United States v. Reorganized CF&I Fabricators of Utah, Inc., No. 95-325; October Term 1995.](../records/United_States_v_Reorganized_CFI_Fabricators_of_Utah_Inc_merits_1996-06-20.md).

##### Opinion Topology

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court, Part I | Souter | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Ginsburg, Breyer | Preserves denial of tax priority | Complete statutory text-and-operation rationale and priority disposition |
| Opinion of the Court, Part II | Souter | Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | Rejects stated equitable subordination and requires remand | Complete equitable-subordination rule and remand on that ground; Thomas does not join Part I's tax treatment |
| Concurrence in part and dissent in part | Thomas | No other Justice | Agrees with Part II; opposes Part I | Federal excise-tax classification and its priority consequence |

##### Separate Writings

Justice Thomas concurs in Part II and dissents from Part I. Congress enacted this federal assessment as a tax properly treated as an excise, and its regulatory or deterrent object does not authorize withdrawing the priority Congress gave excise taxes. He distinguishes the need to prevent a State's label from controlling federal bankruptcy law from the treatment owed Congress's own federal tax choice. The bankruptcy tax inquiry does not, in his view, license the Court to reclassify this federal excise on the majority's functional ground. He would reverse the penalty-based priority ruling and remand consistently with tax treatment, while retaining express Bankruptcy Code limitations; he does not claim that every IRS charge receives priority. He fully agrees that Noland forecloses the stated equitable ground, even for a claim he would classify as a priority tax. His disagreement therefore does not extend to rejection of the challenged subordination, preservation of legally supported statutory equity, or leaving independent plan issues open.


#### Baby Richard, by his guardian ad litem, v. Kirchner (In re Petition of Kirchner); Illinois Supreme Court No. 78101, 164 Ill. 2d 468, 649 N.E.2d 324 (1995); October Term 1995. — 1996-06-21

Authority: [Baby Richard, by his guardian ad litem, v. Kirchner (In re Petition of Kirchner); Illinois Supreme Court No. 78101, 164 Ill. 2d 468, 649 N.E.2d 324 (1995); October Term 1995.](../records/Baby_Richard_v_Kirchner_merits_1996-06-21.md).

##### Opinion Topology

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court, Parts I-II | Stone-Zsela | Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer | Complete protected-interest rule, procedure, limited vacatur and remand |
| Dissent | O'Connor | Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas | Rejects the proposed constitutional predicate on this record; would affirm while preserving state-law measures and different supported constitutional claims |

##### Separate Writings

Justice O'Connor dissents, joined by Justices Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas. The dissent accepts the distinction between implementation and permanent custody but concludes that the established relationship and possible trauma do not supply the new constitutional liberty predicate. Smith did not establish the asserted foster-family interest and gave special weight to restoration of the natural family. Parham and Flores address institutional restraint, a materially different deprivation from placing a child with his fit father.

Mathews selects process for an established interest; the practicality of a modest inquiry cannot establish that interest. Neither state compulsion, the seriousness of possible loss nor a carefully limited remedy is enough. A. St. P. C.'s particular proof requirement and Heller and Foucha's commitment rules cannot be transferred to this setting. DeShaney and Collins caution against turning concern for safety into a general due-process guarantee. Pinder did not decide the outer affirmative-injury merits and supplies no rule resolving them against every claimant.

The dissent would affirm the reviewed federal judgment while leaving humane state-law implementation measures available. It does not infer that Richard will be unharmed, endorse every abrupt transfer, require a factually identical historical precedent, or foreclose a different independently supported constitutional injury. Its common rationale does not adopt Michael H.'s most-specific-tradition method. The disagreement is with the protected-interest predicate here, not with the father's obligation to comply with otherwise lawful child-protection measures.
